901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany1
901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.summary: Abstract Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets*
901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.summary: Abstract This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors*
901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.summary: Abstract People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data*
901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.summary: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches*
901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.summary: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning*
901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.summary: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals ’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard*
901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.summary: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

For 70 years, Lo Scoglio has lured movie stars, billionaires, and locals to a tiny bay on the Amalfi Coast. Now the legendary restaurant is coming to Manhattan, with hundreds of fried zucchini in tow By Joseph Bullmore “T he most beautiful things are the hardest to reach,” says Leonardo Bottone, the manager at Hotel Palazzo Murat, in Positano. He is talking about Lo Scoglio da Tommaso—the restaurant lounging in the neighboring bay of Nerano on a large wooden pier atop a boulder in the sea, as if it simply took a break from swimming to sun itself on the rocks one day and has stayed put ever since. There are no direct ferry services from the main port towns to Nerano, stuck in its little nook on the southern coast of the Sorrento Peninsula. And the road leading down to it zigzags precipitously until it dead-ends somewhere above the water. So you really need a boat (or, better yet, a friend’s) to get there. READ ON

fc4853f6ed:018994ce8e1b26c3.title: To Have and to Hoard
fc4853f6ed:018994ce8e1b26c3.author: Jennifer Noyes
fc4853f6ed:018994ce8e1b26c3.summary: Everything in moderation, including moderation. When does a carefully curated collection become an unruly obsession? By Jennifer Noyes I have a weakness for silver objects. Not silverware, exactly, because that would suggest a degree of practicality, but silver things. Then he led me past the little house, into the backyard, and up a flight of stairs, and I found myself inside a makeshift recording studio that he’d dubbed, with scrupulous irony, “Small Mercies.” READ ON

All-inclusive resorts and private compounds now control more than 99 percent of the country’s world-famous beaches. Ordinary Jamaicans are fed up By Ben Ryder Howe A decade ago, while working for a travel magazine, I got into a conversation one day with a few colleagues about which countries, for moral reasons, we would never write about. One person said Saudi Arabia, until it allowed women to drive. Another mentioned Uganda, or any country that persecuted gays. I wouldn’t have said Jamaica back then; in fact, that year I visited Jamaica and wrote a short, positive piece about one of its hotels. However, today if I had to pick a country whose economy I refuse to support, it would be Jamaica, the island nation long defined by beaming smiles, party music, and the all-inclusive resort model, which it invented. fc4853f6ed:e43fac85e52bfb6e.summary: Ahead of the midterms, a new book of photographs by Jean-Pierre Laffont captures two decades of American defiance By Elena Clavarino P erhaps only a first-generation immigrant can truly understand America. “We are outsiders,” explains Eliane Laffont, wife of the French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont. “Whether we like it or not. You know, we are not your typical Americans, so it’s very easy for us to see what’s good and what’s bad and what’s ugly …” Few have had a better vantage point than Jean-Pierre Laffont. Since his arrival in New York, in 1964, Laffont has photographed America at its most restless, rebellious, and unruly, capturing the civil-rights movement, anti–Vietnam War protesters, hippies turned Rajneeshees in Oregon, the gay-liberation movement, gangs in the Bronx, and the street culture that gave rise to hip-hop. dc01c62177:2aa232ce43926070.summary: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. This paper examines the impact of product market competition on customer-driven taste-based discrimination in a service economy characterized by homophily. I develop a novel equilibrium model of both product and labor markets in which heightened product market competition tends to exacerbate labor market discrimination in customer-facing occupations. dc01c62177:815731a64c87a3a4.summary: I study frictions that prevent financial institutions from granting debt relief to struggling borrowers in the U.S. residential mortgage market. dc01c62177:85c854bd6bd168e1.author: Ann
dc01c62177:85c854bd6bd168e1.summary: What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms’ demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms’ markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. dc01c62177:67e7bad29e054020.author: Ann

dc01c62177:b3bce3a82418275f.author: Ann
dc01c62177:b3bce3a82418275f.summary: Pawn loans offer borrowers a substantial degree of repayment flexibility in exchange for a harsh penalty in case of default: forfeit of collateral worth more than the loan amount along with any payments made toward recovery. Using a large RCT conducted in Mexico City, we document key stylized facts about pawn lending and explore the merits of replacing flexibility with structured repayment contracts in this important but understudied form of credit. dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.author: Ann
dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.summary: Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies — those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. dc01c62177:4d563343f0796d66.author: Ann

dc01c62177:d21547d3a9c0ac9e.author: Ann

0a975616a0:9ab5b4e94d233b91.summary: Loss Of A Legend: Judge Richard Posner died last week leaving an indelible impact on the law and all those he knew. The Juniors Must Go Down With The Ship: As Weil winds down, first-year associates worry the teams heading for the exits aren't saving them a seat. More Bad News On The Horizon? : Meanwhile, eight departed finance partners and some acquisition chatter have Biglaw asking whether Cahill Gordon is next. Hobby Lobby: Judges at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention posted their hobbies on lunch-table signs, and their answers ran the gamut from "America" to "You've Got to Have Hobbies." For textualists they seem wholly incapable of understanding the plain meaning of the request. f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty*
f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.summary: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the Metco Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.summary: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts, to relatively wealthier and predominantly white suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher-achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal*
f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.summary: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.title: Fairness Across the World
f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.summary: Abstract This article provides the first comprehensive global evidence on people’s fairness and efficiency preferences, beliefs about the sources of inequality and the efficiency cost of redistribution, and policy attitudes toward redistribution. Using a globally harmonized consequential experiment with more than 65,000 individuals across 60 countries, we show that the source of inequality plays a substantially larger role for inequality acceptance than the efficiency cost of redistribution. At the global level, implemented inequality increases by 85% when inequality is caused by merit rather than luck, compared with a 14% increase when redistribution entails a 50% efficiency cost. We document substantial heterogeneity in fairness views and beliefs within and across societies. The meritocratic fairness view is most prominent in many richer Western societies, while libertarian and egalitarian fairness views are widespread in many other parts of the world. Globally, people are more likely to believe that inequality reflects luck rather than merit, while beliefs in large efficiency costs of redistribution are relatively weak. Fairness preferences and beliefs are strongly associated with redistribution attitudes and actual redistribution through taxes and transfers across countries. Our findings illustrate how the interaction between fairness views and beliefs may shape redistribution across societies, highlighting the importance of jointly understanding preferences and beliefs in the political economy of redistribution.

f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.title: Wealth and Property Taxation in the United States*
f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.summary: Abstract We study the history and geography of wealth accumulation in the United States using newly collected historical property tax records from the early 1800s onward. These records come from the administration of the General Property Tax—a tax that aspired to cover all types of property. We construct wealth series at the state, county, and national levels. At the state level, we use annual assessed values of wealth from state-level reports drawn from multiple sources. Because assessed values may differ from market values, we also require assessment ratios, defined as the ratio of assessed to market wealth. We obtain state-level assessment ratios from decadal U.S. Census wealth data (drawn from various census reports, including those on “Wealth, Debt, and Taxation”), in which the census carried out detailed valuation work, complemented with information on changes in assessment practices from the state reports, to build higher-frequency series of assessment ratios. The result is long-run annual wealth series for states from 1850 (or earlier, depending on the state) to 1935. We obtain national wealth series by aggregating these state series. At the county level, we use assessed values (or market values where available) from the U.S. Census wealth data for each decade and apply either state-level or county-level assessment ratios, where available, to obtain market values of wealth for each decade from 1850 to 1930. We use these data to show, first, that the United States experienced extraordinary wealth accumulation after the Civil War and until the Great Depression. Second, spatial inequality in the United States has been large and highly persistent since the mid-1800s. We also examine the determinants of long-term wealth growth and find, among other results, that counties with a higher share of enslaved property before the Civil War or with higher wealth inequality experienced lower subsequent long-run wealth growth.

56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.author: Xu, Yaling
56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.author: Hellsten, Mark
56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.author: Xiaoqing Zhou
56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.summary: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.title: Job Characteristics That Matter for Women : Evidence from a Large-Scale Experiment in Pakistan
56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.author: Tas, Emcet Oktay
56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.summary: In the presence of gender-specific barriers, certain workplace environments and amenities may be particularly important for women, yet difficult to observe during job search due to information frictions. A large-scale field experiment on Pakistan's online job board publicized these job characteristics—namely, supervisor gender, coworker gender composition, work flexibility, commuting support, and overnight travel requirements. Information on these characteristics was randomly disclosed in job advertisements and email alerts. Analysis at the job-alert level shows that female jobseekers respond to supervisor gender, remote work, and commuting support. At the job level, when these characteristics were disclosed, the number of female applicants increased as the jobs were more favorable to women.

56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.title: Immigrant-Native Wage Gaps and Rent Sharing: A Segmented Assimilation Story?
56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.author: Mélanie Volral
56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.summary: Although an increasing body of literature has examined the relationship between firms’ profitability and wage inequality in the context of a diverse workforce, the role of rent sharing in explaining origin-based wage differentials has yet to be explored. Our paper aims to fill this gap using detailed Belgian matched employer-employee data from 1999 to 2016. After controlling for a wide range of covariates and addressing endogeneity issues, our estimates show that the wage-profit elasticity equals approximately 3% and does not differ statistically between native and immigrant workers, be they first or second generation. It therefore appears that firms share their profits equally with their employees, regardless of their origin. However, Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions suggest that rent sharing has a significant influence on immigrants’ wages through labour market segregation. Specifically, first-generation immigrants are found to earn lower wages than natives because of their higher concentration in firms with lower profit margins. The same is true for second-generation immigrants, but almost half as much. These findings, corroborated and refined by heterogeneity tests according to gender, educational attainment and level of collective bargaining, support the hypothesis of a segmented assimilation process for immigrants.

56c7f0b50e:00819b0aa70bab01.title: Parental job loss across child age and human capital formation
56c7f0b50e:00819b0aa70bab01.author: Alexander Willén

56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.title: Representation over Rents: Labor Market Beliefs and the Gender Wage Gap
56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.author: Ana Figueiredo
56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.summary: We study how labor market beliefs shape the gender wage gap in an equilibrium search model with endogenous wage setting and hiring, in which workers hold subjective expectations about wage offers, job arrival rates, and separation risk. Using data from the Survey of Consumer Expectations to estimate the model, we find that gender differences in beliefs account for 25% of the gender wage gap. Correcting these beliefs partly narrows the gap but is not welfare-improving, as it reduces lifetime earnings for both men and women. In contrast, equalizing labor market fundamentals substantially reduces the wage gap while increasing women's lifetime earnings.

4bca44730b:34d7e3f243f58535.title: Speaking Engagements/Conferences
4bca44730b:34d7e3f243f58535.author: Francine

4bca44730b:39462350981770e8.title: My take on the latest at the PCAOB and KPMG
4bca44730b:39462350981770e8.author: Francine

4bca44730b:e00b3f3b66af829c.author: Francine

0cf31f7a1a:29ca41aefe94d1e4.title: Gender Identity and Recorded Offending: Evidence from Linked Population Data
0cf31f7a1a:29ca41aefe94d1e4.author: Alexander Plum
0cf31f7a1a:29ca41aefe94d1e4.summary: Population evidence on gender identity and offending remains scarce. We link New Zealand’s 2023 Census to administrative records for 170, 775 New Zealand-born individuals from the 1993–1998 birth cohorts. Separate measures of sex at birth and gender distinguish six groups: cisgender women, cisgender men, transgender women, transgender men, and nonbinary individuals grouped by sex assigned at birth. Their histories of selected Police-recorded interpersonal and victim-related offenses are examined over a common ten-year window at ages 17–26. Adjusting for ethnicity, parental income, parental sentencing history, and year-month of birth, all four gender-minority groups have significantly lower odds of a qualifying record than cisgender men. For transgender women, the adjusted probability is 5.1%, compared with 12.2% for cisgender men and 6.0% for cisgender women. The corresponding differences are −7.2 and −1.0 percentage points; only the former is statistically significant. Across the main analyses of offense type, court action, victim characteristics, and location, transgender women consistently have lower adjusted probabilities than cisgender men, while differences from cisgender women are not statistically significant. These findings document variation in recorded offending obscured by conventional binary classifications.

0cf31f7a1a:996325d3194ef715.title: External Shocks and Police Behaviour: Evidence from Terrorist Attacks in the UK
0cf31f7a1a:996325d3194ef715.author: Gennaro Rossi
0cf31f7a1a:996325d3194ef715.summary: Shocks, such as terrorist attacks, may shift policing through profiling (group-targeted enforcement driven by salience) or operational changes. We test these channels using administrative data from Londonâ€™s Metropolitan Police Service on use-of-force incidents and stop-and-searches, linked to UK terrorist attacks between April 2017 and November 2019. Exploiting attack timing in a regression discontinuity-in-time design, we compare outcomes in narrow windows around each event. Across both datasets we find little evidence of short-run ethnic profiling after Muslim extremist or far-right attacks. In contrast, Muslim extremist attacks â€“ substantially more lethal in our sample â€“ are followed by a shift toward weapons searches, more public-protection-focused force, and greater use-of-force intensity for both White and Non-white subjects. The evidence is consistent with heightened alertness rather than discriminatory targeting.

0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.title: The Aftermath of the 2024 UK Riots: Reporting on Social Media, Misinformation, and Crime
0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.author: James Moir
0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.summary: On 30th July 2024, the UK saw its worst riots in over a decade following a knife attack in Southport that left three girls dead and ten injured. False claims about the attacker being a Muslim asylum seeker spread rapidly online, turning vigils into violence as far-right groups used X, TikTok and Telegram to coordinate attacks on mosques, asylum centres and local businesses. Many of the rioters received prison sentences for arson and racially aggravated offences. Information disorder played a central role in the 2024 riots, both triggering unrest and intensifying violence through the rapid dissemination of false narratives. Disinformation acted as the initial spark, later transforming into misinformation as unaware individuals reshared it. Social media sites such as Telegram involved the sharing of extremist material that merged transnational and domestic narratives. Global disinformation and local grievances became intertwined, merging foreign interference with home-grown mobilisation. As the riots took place there was evidence an online-offline feedback loop which resulted in prosecutions that relied heavily on digital evidence. This paper examines a corpus of newspaper reports on the issue of social media, disinformation, and crime in the ensuing two-year period since the riots. The news media sources were derived from a search using LexisNexis, a web-based archive of news titles in the UK. This is involved a selective search of news from the range of broadsheet and tabloid titles across the political spectrum. The key search terms were ?Stockport?, ?riots? ?social media?, ?misinformation?, ?disinformation? and ?police?. A discourse analytic approach was applied to the reports that reveal the different political stances taken on the issue of social media, misinformation, and crime. These are bound up with rhetorical constructions concerning the release of police information on the identities of alleged offenders, the control of social media, and social and…

0cf31f7a1a:61ebb4831b764bf1.title: Public salience mobilizes nationwide responses to violence against women
0cf31f7a1a:61ebb4831b764bf1.author: Gabriele Pinto
0cf31f7a1a:61ebb4831b764bf1.summary: Does public salience around femicides mobilize societal responses or trigger further harm through imitation? Using newly assembled case-level data on femicides in Italy from 2017 to 2024, we study the nationwide consequences of the most salient cases for help-seeking, police reporting, and lethal violence. We find that highly salient intimate partner femicides (IPFs) generate nationwide increases in help-seeking, and that an exceptionally salient IPF also leads to a marked rise in police reports of violence against women. Yet we find no evidence of an increase in femicides-a pattern inconsistent with copycat theories. Responses are strongest during periods of peak salience. No comparable mobilization follows a lower-salience IPF, a similarly salient femicide committed by family members, a highly salient killing of a woman not classified as a femicide, or a lower-salience falsification case. Together, these comparisons indicate that mobilization depends on salience intensity, the victim-perpetrator relationship, and the gendered nature of the violence, rather than reflecting a generic response to salient violent crime. These findings suggest that public salience can contribute to prevention strategies against gender-based violence without amplifying lethal violence.

0cf31f7a1a:7fc06c652dbd03a7.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
0cf31f7a1a:7fc06c652dbd03a7.author: María Micaela Sviatschi
0cf31f7a1a:7fc06c652dbd03a7.summary: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2, 500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

0cf31f7a1a:6ba77cb5cb954f9c.title: Policy Evaluation Beyond Significance Testing: Evidence from Chicago's ShotSpotter Contract
0cf31f7a1a:6ba77cb5cb954f9c.author: Adam K. Soliman
0cf31f7a1a:6ba77cb5cb954f9c.summary: Program impact estimates that are not statistically significant are often treated as providing little guidance for policy choice, even when economically important effects remain plausible. In such cases, the decision-relevant task is not simply to test whether the effect differs from zero, but to estimate the probability distribution of programmatic effects. The importance of going beyond hypothesis testing is especially clear when evaluations are underpowered relative to the effect needed for benefits to exceed costs. We illustrate this point using Chicago’s contract for ShotSpotter, an acoustical gunshot detection system that reduces police response times and may therefore have improved survival among shooting victims. Using a geographic RD design, we estimate that ShotSpotter reduced the shooting fatality rate by 2.5 percentage points, equivalent to roughly 49 fewer deaths per year. Although the estimate is not statistically significant, its implied benefit far exceeds the cost of the service. To have enough statistical power under the hypothesis testing approach to detect an effect of this size would require 87 years’ worth of Chicago shooting data. We instead implement a decision-relevant perspective using Bayesian analysis, treating the life-saving effect as a random variable. We find positive expected net benefits, with posterior probabilities that benefits exceed costs ranging from 70% under a flat prior and a $0.5 million value of statistical life to 99.6% under a no-harm prior and a $13.6 million value. The results illustrate how reliance on statistical significance can discard decision-relevant evidence when economically meaningful effects are difficult to detect precisely.

0cf31f7a1a:b34885efce18c31f.title: Unlawful Tariffs: Incidence, Damages, and Remedies
0cf31f7a1a:b34885efce18c31f.author: Gunner Heins
0cf31f7a1a:b34885efce18c31f.summary: In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the Supreme Court held that the tariffs imposed by executive order pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act exceeded presidential authority. The decision has generated over two thousand lawsuits and potential refund exposure in the range of $130–175 billion. This Article provides a law and economics analysis of the recovery problem. Drawing on the Bigelow measure of antitrust damages and standard tax incidence theory, the Article argues that both importers and foreign exporters have suffered cognizable injury. The damage suffered by each class depends on the incidence of the tariff, which is determined by the elasticities of domestic import demand and foreign export supply. The Article examines the complications introduced by market power, supply-chain pass-on under Illinois Brick, the problem of windfalls, and the econometric challenges of estimating the but-for price. Methodological approaches—including before-and-after comparisons, yardstick methods, and structural demand estimation—are evaluated. The Article also addresses the social welfare loss not captured by private damage claims and the procedural constraint imposed by the 180-day customs protest period.

0cf31f7a1a:a566b75bcbf21f4a.title: Large Language Models and Ottoman Court Records: Long-Term Change and Regional Comparison
0cf31f7a1a:a566b75bcbf21f4a.author: Metin M. Cosgel
0cf31f7a1a:a566b75bcbf21f4a.summary: Large language models offer new ways to turn historical texts into quantitative evidence, but their value depends on whether the resulting data support reliable comparisons. I examine that potential through Ottoman court registers, a source for studying long-term change and regional variation after regular tax surveys ceased around 1600. I combine rule-based extraction with large language models to convert 385 transcribed volumes from twelve districts into a dataset of 160, 395 entries. Rules extract formulaic information, while models classify documents, identify participants’ roles, and interpret legal outcomes. Validation uses hand-coded samples and comparisons with three published Istanbul studies of intergenerational persistence of social standing, foreign-coin use, and the decisive oath in litigation. The new extraction recovers their principal patterns and adds later observations to the standing and oath series. Applying common definitions across districts reveals different relationships between the capital and the provinces. The oath’s early seventeenth-century peak and subsequent decline appear broadly across the observed courts. Foreign silver accounted for substantial shares of recorded transaction value earlier in Antep, Amasya, and Kayseri than in Istanbul and several western and central districts. The early seventeenth-century decline in father–son status persistence in Istanbul was shared by Bursa but was not a general provincial pattern. Uneven transcription coverage, selection into court, and extraction error limit these comparisons. Within those limits, the method makes published court records usable for comparative quantitative history across several centuries and regions.

0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.title: Demystifying Unconscionability: A Historical and Empirical Analysis
0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.author: McCall, Brian M.
0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.summary: The doctrine of unconscionability is encrusted with myths. First-year law students are taught that the doctrine was created in the twentieth century. Unconscionability is often presented as a novel one, born in the Uniform Commercial Code’s adoption of Section 2-302 in the mid-twentieth century. Even those scholars who are willing to look a bit further afield than the twentieth century for the origins of the unconscionability doctrine typically only reach the mid-eighteenth century. In addition to myths surrounding its origin, the doctrine has been presented as a dangerously vague and imprecise concept. Commentators and scholars have likewise characterized the doctrine as a license for courts to refuse, unpredictably and arbitrarily, to enforce some contracts. Some claim its application has the potential to destroy all of contract law. Beyond the fearmongering myths, another standard myth taught to first-year law students is that to succeed on a claim of unconscionability a party must offer at least some proof of both procedural and substantive unconscionability. This Article will thus attempt to dispel the following three myths about unconscionability: • It is a new, modern doctrine of law, • Its application is unpredictable and arbitrary, and • To prevail a party must prove both procedural and substantive unconscionability. The best way to dispel myths is through facts. This Article attempts to clear the clouds of confusion and fear surrounding the doctrine by turning to historical and empirical fact. Part I of this Article looks to the ancient past and finds that the idea that justice, and hence the law, should grant a remedy to at least some people who enter into inequitable bargains, is as old as philosophizing about justice itself (and certainly older than the mid-eighteenth century). Rather than a dangerous modern innovation, this principle of justice has ancient philosophical roots in Aristotle and ancient legal roots in Roman law. Part II of the Article…

0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.title: When Crime Enters City Hall: Organized Crime and Municipal Finance in Mexico
0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.author: Cesar Velazquez
0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.summary: Criminal organizations can affect local state capacity not only through violence but also through their interaction with local governments. This article examines whether criminal presence affects municipal public finances. Using 24 years of public finance data for the universe of Mexican municipalities and an event-study design, we exploit the timing of the first recorded presence of a criminal organization. We find that criminal presence is associated with lower unearmarked expenditures, driven particularly by a decline in absolute public investment and its share of total expenditure. Although the budget shares allocated to general services, personnel services, and transfers and subsidies increase, these changes do not necessarily reflect increases in absolute spending. We find no evidence of a change in own-source revenues, except in municipalities where only newly created criminal organizations are present, which exhibit higher own-source revenues. The contraction in expenditure is concentrated in municipalities with high criminal fragmentation and in those where historical criminal organizations are present. Overall, the findings indicate that organized crime is associated with a contraction in municipal expenditure and a change in budget composition.

0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.title: Dismissing Human Trafficking: Forced Arbitration of Survivors’ Civil Suits
0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.author: Werner, Daniel
0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.summary: For more than two decades, federal law has provided trafficked individuals the right to sue their traffickers in court and hundreds of survivors have filed suit. Their litigation has yielded millions in judgments and settlements, public accountability, development of the law, and a deeper understanding of human trafficking. Forced arbitration of human trafficking claims threatens these successes. Much has been written about the existence and enforcement of pre-dispute arbitration clauses, particularly in employment and consumer matters. This Article is the first to assess these pervasive contractual provisions in the context of human trafficking. It sets out the public and private functions of the federal private right of action for trafficking survivors. Informed by federal cases where alleged traffickers successfully compelled arbitration, the Article details how these important functions are undermined by forced arbitration and how the harms of human trafficking are exacerbated by it. Compelling arbitration of survivors’ civil claims erodes government efforts to combat human trafficking and to support survivors. This Article makes two recommendations to address this deepening and underappreciated problem. First, Congress should amend the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) to invalidate pre-dispute arbitration provisions in cases involving human trafficking. Second, the regulations governing temporary work visas for foreign nationals should prohibit pre-dispute arbitration provisions in their employment contracts. In the meantime, survivors can continue to challenge these provisions in court using contract defenses.

0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.title: First-Month Check-Ins as an Early Indicator in Pretrial Supervision
0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.author: Warren, Madeline
0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.summary: Pretrial supervision has a short window to keep a person on track to resolve their case without returning to jail, and most of what agencies use to set supervision intensity is fixed at booking. Published pretrial research has found static factors such as criminal history and prior failures to appear more predictive than dynamic ones (Bechtel, Lowenkamp, & Holsinger, 2011), but the findings reported here may challenge that conclusion. This paper asks whether something RePath records from the first day of supervision, the share of scheduled app check-ins a participant completes in the first 30 days, says anything about how the case ends. We examined Missouri pretrial cases across 65 agencies that closed successfully or unsuccessfully between October 1, 2025 and September 30, 2026 and were open at least 30 days (4, 833 closures). Among the 1, 504 cases with check-ins scheduled in the first month, participants whose cases closed successfully had completed 68.9% of them and those whose cases closed unsuccessfully 47.3%, a gap of 21.6 points (95% CI 17.2 to 26.0; Cohen's d = 0.67). Participants who completed fewer than half closed unsuccessfully 32.9% of the time, against 14.2% for the rest (risk ratio 2.31). The unsuccessful-closure rate was highest among participants who completed little or none of their first-month check-ins (39.5% at zero) and lowest among those who completed nearly all of them (7.9% at 90–99%; none of 26 at 100%), and first-month completion separated outcomes with an AUC of .69 (95% CI .66 to .72), within the range reported for two validated pretrial risk tools, the Public Safety Assessment (.55–.68) and the federal Pretrial Risk Assessment (.67–.73), though the populations, outcomes and timing differ. The gap held across case-length floors, within agencies, and with excluded closures recoded either way. We report the result with its boundaries: one state, one year, outcomes as provided by agencies, technical revocations and new arrests not…

0cf31f7a1a:323b1a0617ef6c8c.title: Crime and prices: thefts of expensive precious metals from cars
0cf31f7a1a:323b1a0617ef6c8c.author: Sandi, Matteo
0cf31f7a1a:323b1a0617ef6c8c.summary: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.

0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.title: Can Civic Mobilization Reduce Sexual Violence? Evidence from March 4 Justice Demonstrations in Australia
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.author: Astghik Mavisakalyan
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.summary: Civic mobilization is a common societal response to gender-based violence, but whether it actually changes sexual offending is largely unknown. We exploit geographic variation in exposure to the March 4 Justice (M4J) movement — a nationally coordinated series of protests against gender-based violence held across Australia on 15th March 2021 — as a natural experiment, using a difference-in-differences design. We find that areas hosting the protests experienced a 16 to 21 per cent reduction in recorded sexual assaults over the six to twelve months following the movement, with no significant effects across six other crime categories. This suggests a mechanism specific to sexual violence rather than general deterrence. These effects are larger in locations closer to protest activity and at sites with sizable crowds compared to smaller ones. Attitudinal data from the National Community Attitudes towards Violence against Women Survey reveal significant shifts in men’s attitudes: greater rejection of rape myths, increased survivor credibility, and reduced endorsement of patriarchal norms, with these shifts concentrated among younger and more educated men. The reductions in sexual assault are concentrated in male-represented areas, where the movement’s normative signal was more novel, and nationwide, we find suggestive evidence of a modest rise in female electoral support in 2022 relative to 2019. Together, these findings suggest that civic mobilization can reduce violence through the internalization of norms.

ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.author: Ana Popovici
ef78496c13:0a791fc2c22af02e.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.title: The Transparency Tax : Discouraging Firm Ownership via Tax Havens
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.author: Bajaña, Alex
ef78496c13:98521d54d58b6699.summary: Tax havens weaken tax enforcement by obscuring firm ownership and facilitating offshore evasion. This paper studies a reform in Ecuador that imposed a corporate tax surcharge on firms with owners in tax havens, using a newly available ownership registry. Comparing haven-owned firms to other foreign-owned firms, the analysis finds that the reform reduced haven ownership by 12 percentage points, largely through disclosure of non-haven individual owners. Exposed firms reduced transactions with tax havens and increased corporate tax payments, with no detectable effects on investment or firm size. The results suggest that ownership transparency can meaningfully improve tax compliance at limited efficiency cost, even through unilateral action.

ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.title: Partners on a Climb : Financial Sector Development and Tax Collections in Indonesia
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.author: Polat, Beyza
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.summary: Shallow financial markets may act as an important structural constraint on a country’s ability to mobilize tax revenues. This paper explores this hypothesis in the context of Indonesia, a middle-income country with persistently low tax collections and low financial sector depth. At the macro level, relating cross-country financial development to new estimates of tax gaps, it finds that a 1 percent increase in private credit as a share of GDP could reduce the tax gap by approximately 0.2 percent. At the micro level, analysis of publicly listed Indonesian companies suggests that a one-decile increase in financial constraints is associated with a 0.18 percentage point drop in cash effective tax rates, indicating that financially constrained firms may be using tax planning as a liquidity tool. The results suggest that tax collections are positively associated with financial sector deepening.

ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.title: Low fertility rates: A fiscal policy perspective
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.author: Baur, Martin
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.summary: Switzerland’s fertility rate fell below 1.3 children per woman in 2024 and has remained well below the replacement level for decades, reflecting a broader trend across advanced economies. This paper discusses the economic and fiscal implications of persistently low fertility, reviews its underlying causes and the extent to which family policy can influence fertility decisions, and presents policy options available for Switzerland. Low fertility slows growth of the domestic working-age population, accelerates population ageing, and reduces long-term economic growth potential. For public finances, it dampens tax revenues and social insurance contributions while increasing age-related expenditure, particularly on pensions and healthcare. The causes of low fertility are multifaceted, including the financial costs of having children, difficulties in reconciling work and family life, and broader changes in social norms and lifestyles. Evidence from OECD countries suggests that family policies can alleviate some constraints, but their effects on fertility are small and often temporary. Coherent and well-coordinated measures supporting families throughout the child-rearing years appear more promising than individual measures. As a sustained reversal of current fertility trends appears unlikely, economic and fiscal policy should focus on adapting to an ageing society by making better use of the domestic labour supply, facilitating labor-market-oriented immigration, and fostering productivity growth. Finally, reforms to strengthen the fiscal sustainability of pension and healthcare systems become even more important.

ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.title: The Fiscal Alibi: Hidden Spending Needs and Government Reputation
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.summary: A government may ask for a high tax because it faces a genuine expense. The same demand can also be made by a government that intends to keep the proceeds. We study this ambiguity in a two-period reputation model with privately observed spending needs and an endogenous tax base. The opportunist chooses between outright confiscation and levies that an honest government might impose. We characterize the three possible regimes through a single equilibrium equation. A mean-preserving spread of legitimate needs weakly raises the opportunist’s lifetime value, with a strict increase precisely when the spread changes the upper tail relevant for mimicry. We then give a necessary and sufficient curvature condition for this ordering to extend to a general reputational continuation prize. Verification reduces the value of concealment, but also changes how the opportunist extracts. In the benchmark economy, greater auditing weakly lowers current citizen welfare, even before audit costs, while improving the future allocation through better information. The welfare case for verification consequently depends on the balance between these two effects. Examples yield no auditing, an optimum within a regime, and an optimum at the boundary between regimes.

ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.title: Taxing Capital to Protect It
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.summary: This paper studies the composition of taxation when the government cannot fully commit to respecting private returns after investment. A fiscal authority must finance a given expenditure from labor and capital income. Ordinary tax receipts are protected, but an opportunistic executive can seize part of the remaining capital payment. We show that a revenue-neutral increase in the capital tax raises the probability of compliance whenever the labor tax is below its local, fixedwage revenue peak, provided the equilibrium remains on a regular mixing branch. This result does not depend on the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor. The same reform can raise investment: the gain in expected retention must outweigh the decline in the opportunist’s continuation gain as compliance becomes less informative. We also characterize the Ramsey allocation conditional on full compliance. Limited commitment then imposes a ceiling on sustainable capital payments, rather than a general lower bound on the statutory capital-tax rate. Finally, we distinguish a change in the authority’s concern for the future from an increase in both actors’ patience. The former favors more informative policies when continuation welfare is convex; the latter has no unconditional direction in the reduced-form policy problem.

ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.title: Tax Expenditure Reporting as a Commitment Device for Revenue Mobilization
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.author: Gaël Tape
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.summary: This note shows that publishing tax expenditure reports increases tax revenue mobilization over the medium term in emerging and developing countries. The results indicate that this effect emerges six to seven years after publication and is driven primarily by direct taxes. The effect is stronger when reports are published more frequently and on a regular basis. It is also more pronounced in low-income countries and in sub-Saharan Africa. Publishing tax expenditure reports acts as a commitment mechanism. By making tax exemptions visible, it raises the political cost of opaque exemptions and gradually strengthens the government's capacity to steer tax policy.

ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.title: The Strange and Curious Tax Treatment of Investment Expenses
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.author: Morris, Mallory A.
ef78496c13:15013f601580df67.summary: To secure income, taxpayers often incur a wide range of expenses. At least theoretically, one might think that the Internal Revenue Code (“Code”) would accord all such expenses similar tax treatment, but (i) trade or business expenses and (ii) investment expenses endure the exact opposite tax treatment: the former are generally allowed, whereas the latter are commonly disallowed. The obvious question is why there is a difference in treatment between the two. This Article explores possible answers to that important question. It first traces the evolution of the Code’s dichotomous tax treatment of trade or business versus investment expenses. It then investigates possible justifications and their associated merits for the different handling of these two expense categories. With this background information in mind, to make the tax system more administrable, equitable, and efficient, this Article advocates for the deductibility of investment expenses and describes several beneficial implications associated with the institution of this proposed reform

ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.title: Workplace Transformation And Its Tax Compliance Implications
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.author: Soled, Jay A.
ef78496c13:d93526d5ab31cb29.summary: Due to technological advances and the COVID-19 pandemic, taxpayers are increasingly utilizing their homes as a focal point from which to conduct their business affairs. On the one hand, the nation should applaud this workplace transformation insofar as it may enhance job performance and efficiency, reduce product cost and overhead, and improve work-life balance. On the other hand, this transformation process may open the door to rampant tax abuse as taxpayers alone or in collusion with their employers seek to transform home usage into a tax shelter refuge. This analysis delves directly into the income tax compliance concerns that the workplace transformation engenders. It does so by exposing the nature of the problem, its prevalence, what it might cost the nation annually in terms of lost revenue, and why current safeguards are failing to achieve their sought-after objectives. The good news is that if Congress proactively takes immediate remedial measures to address this nascent problem, such actions could help foster taxpayer compliance, defend the income tax base, and halt the depletion of the nation’s revenue coffers. However, if Congress dallies and is derelict in fulfilling its oversight duties, this problem is poised to go from bad to worse.

ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.title: AI subsidies as a tool for redistribution
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.author: Lucas Parmentier
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.summary: I study the optimal taxation of artificial intelligence (AI). My analysis highlights a wage-compression effect that provides a rationale for subsidizing AI, as AI adoption may reduce rather than increase wage inequality. When this effect outweighs AI's social costs, AI should be subsidized instead of taxed. I treat AI as a productive input distinct from robots, as the two technologies perform different ranges of tasks. Using numerical simulations, I demonstrate that the optimal policy for AI may differ sharply from that for robots. Under the benchmark calibration, AI is subsidized, whereas robots are taxed. Therefore, the case for taxing AI is weaker than is commonly assumed. When AI lowers the skill premium, fiscal policy may need to encourage, rather than slow, adoption.

ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.title: Perverse Tax Incentives and the Destruction of Creative Works
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.author: Maher, Luke
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.summary: In late 2023, Warner Bros. Discovery announced that it would be permanently shelving Coyote vs. Acme, a complete and hotly anticipated film about popular Looney Tunes characters. This announcement was widely understood—and admitted by Warner Bros. Discovery in its Securities and Exchange Commission filings—to be motivated, at least in part, by a desire to “write off” the film’s costs for tax purposes. This Article is the first to (1) provide a full account for the tax rules that govern what constitutes a “loss” for purposes of unreleased creative works, (2) evaluate whether those rules make sense from both a technical and policy perspective (concluding that they do not), and (3) compare the relative merit of other approaches to allowing tax losses for unreleased creative works. In so doing, this Article makes two necessary contributions to current tax scholarship: first, it links the robust property scholarship on waste to tax policy, setting forth a framework through which critical reappraisals of long-entrenched tax laws and policies can be conducted, identifying ossified policies that no longer comport with our policy goals and revenue-raising needs and developing ways to improve them. Second, it also offers guidance in the ways that the law can think about the ownership, abandonment, and taxation of intangible assets.

b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!

b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.summary: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. The AI Transition My journey on AI started with a selfish and narrow intent, which was to evaluate an investment I had made in Nvidia in 2018, for reasons entirely unrelated to AI. I thought that Nvidia, at the time, was a…

That is why I made my model open to changes that you can make to my story and inputs, and while you have to trust my mechanics, I tried to carry your inputs into value. Much of the pushback I have received has been thoughtful and productive, some of it has been emotional (either from people who love Anthropic or from those who would not touch it with a ten-foot pole) and some of it, especially on the cost of capital, reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and just basic business sense. I plan to play devil's advocate with my own valuation, looking at my story inputs, and ranking them in order of fragility, partly to stress-test my value estimate and partly to reinforce some corporate finance first principles, and then move on to your feedback and what I take away from it. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing. b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.summary: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs) rather than total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows.
