Here, ironically, Arnoldian jurisprudence would be transmogrified into the doctrinaire company-over-country market fundamentalism of the Chicago School of Economics. Today, writes Richard R. John, as we envision for the 21st century a new pro-market, pro-freedom, pro-national security industrial policy, it is worth recalling how U. S. economic development took the form that it did, why the Chicago School repudiated the enduring wisdom of Adam Smith, and what this portends for the world of today. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.title: How George Stigler and the Chicago School Opened the Marketplace of Ideas to Business
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.author: Edward Nik-Khah
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.summary: Henry Simons, the “Crown Prince” of the Chicago School and a professor in the economics department and the law school prior to World War II, sought to develop a laissez faire economics program devoted to eliminating monopoly and pursuing egalitarian goals. George Stigler and the Chicago School abandoned Simons’s anti-monopoly and egalitarian program. The best market became one driven by the search for profits, and the best-functioning marketplace of ideas arose where winning ideas reflected the greater funding backing them, writes Edward Nik-Khah. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.title: The Chicago School Abandoned the Positive Freedom of Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.author: Maha Rafi Atal
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.summary: Adam Smith’s theory of political economy did not begin with the isolated individual but rather the individual who operates to earn the respect of others. Wealth and freedom grew from these relationships and engaging with others to create a free society, or what 20th century philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s would call positive freedom. In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Chicago School abandoned this aspect of freedom in preference of the isolated individual, which in turn produced a weaker concept of freedom, morality, and society that has stifled the cultivation of all three in the United States, writes Maha Rafi Atal. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.title: Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy Complicates Interpretations by the Chicago School and Its Critics
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.author: Sandra Peart and David Levy
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.summary: The connections between Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Theory of Moral Sentiments reveal a much more complicated understanding of how markets work than developed in the common interpretation by the Chicago School of economics or that of its critics. Smith’s political economy based on commerce, sympathy, and competition produced social good but only when complemented and checked by other forces. When not checked, Smith worried about “factions” that produce bad outcomes, write Sandra J. Peart and David M. Levy. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.title: Why Economics Forsook Democracy
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.author: Robert Van Horn
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.summary: The post-World War II Chicago School of Aaron Director and Milton Friedman reimagined a new (neo) liberalism that treated economic liberties and the free market as the greatest defense of political rights. The government, and democracy, were more often than not barriers to economic liberties. The United States continues to suffer from neoliberalism’s prescriptions, and addressing the concerns of today’s populist movements will mean rediscovering ideas of freedom that the Chicago School denigrated, writes Robert Van Horn. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.title: The University of Chicago Once Studied a Laissez-Faire Economics Compatible with Public Interest
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.author: David Mitch
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.summary: The Chicago School is often associated with laissez-faire economics that reads into Adam Smith’s philosophy of political economy justifications for self-interest and prudential motivations. However, a careful history of the University of Chicago’s early Economics Department and School of Commerce and Administration reveals a more complicated understanding of how economics and business were to interact with one another and society. The early University of Chicago pursued a program that emphasized that laissez-faire economics and a concern for the public interest were not antagonists but perfectly compatible, writes David Mitch. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.title: America Became Rich Because of Liberalism
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.author: Peter J. Boettke
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.summary: Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers envisioned a society in which economic and political freedom, grouped together in the ideology of liberalism, would produce a wealthy, free, and peaceful society. Centuries later, this vision has come to fruition, and F. A. Hayek and Milton Friedman helped elaborate and advance that vision in their economic and philosophical works. The lesson for today’s populist moment is not to abandon these principles, but to continue to pursue them, as it is their imperfect realization, not their imperfect conceptualization, that burdens today’s society, writes Peter Boettke. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.title: American Antitrust Has Yet To Figure Out Conglomerates
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.author: Paul Friederiszick
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.summary: The Neo-Brandeisians and Chicago School have employed different statistics to show respectively that markets are both concentrated and not concentrated, leaving Americans in the dark about who really holds corporate power. The evidence only looks contradictory due to the failure of American antitrust scholarship and regulation to understand how conglomerates collect market power across many neighboring markets, through what Paul Friederiszick calls “adjacent market takeovers.” This strategy can make firms more efficient, but it can also raise prices and weaken competition even as each individual market still looks competitive, he writes, drawing on his new paper, “The Conglomerate Power Puzzle.” Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:ad66736fb16d41a6.title: Replacing Credit and Debit Cards With Account-to-Account Payments Would Save Americans Billions

1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.title: Two Questions Determine Whether a Pricing Algorithm Becomes Evidence of Price Fixing
1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.author: Roger D. Blair and Javier D. Donna
1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.summary: Two recent court rulings on casino-hotels using a shared software to fix prices reveal the importance of information exchanges as a super plus factor: an indicator of illegal conspiracy to limit trade. 1aa97d921e:ef855389029b02b3.title: The Foreignness of Africa’s Startup Ecosystem

59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.title: Supporting into-work benefit reform in Spain
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.author: OECD
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.summary: In Spain, the Complemento de Apoyo al Empleo (CAE) allows individuals to receive unemployment benefits whilst in employment. This paper sets out the findings and recommendations of a project aimed at improving the CAE, drawing on international good practice, as well as analyses carried out using the OECD TaxBen model and administrative data. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance – by linking its amount either to UI entitlements or directly to the previous wage – would provide stronger work incentives when wage loss at re-employment is greater; and would limit low-wage traps for full-time workers. However, such reforms would tend to offer lower net income and weaker work incentives for workers transitioning between two low-paid jobs, compared with the current CAE. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance would also increase CAE coverage among re-employed individuals and, consequently, fiscal costs, albeit to a moderate extent. Higher CAE coverage would particularly benefit certain vulnerable groups whose coverage is currently relatively low, such as the low skilled, the youth, and workers in southern regions.

59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.title: Return-to-Work Policies for Disability Insurance Recipients: The Role of Financial Incentives
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.author: Tojerow, Ilan
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.summary: This paper studies how financial incentives shape labor supply decisions among disability insurance (DI) recipients who already combine benefits with part-time work. We exploit a distinctive feature of the Belgian Adapted Work Program, in which DI benefits are progressively withdrawn as earnings increase and the marginal withdrawal rate rises sharply at predefined thresholds. Because participants cannot freely adjust their working hours, this setting allows us to estimate how higher implicit taxation affects transitions out of partial work. Using administrative data and a Regression Kink Design, we find that higher implicit tax rates induce exits in two opposite directions: toward full-time employment and back to full DI. A oneeuro increase in the implicit marginal tax per working day raises the probability of returning to full DI by 3.0 percentage points and of resuming full-time employment by 1.5 percentage points, corresponding to elasticities of 0.84 and 0.85. A simple labor supply framework rationalizes these divergent responses. Our findings show that the financial design of partial-benefit schemes can determine whether partial work serves as a bridge toward full employment or instead leads recipients back to full benefit dependency.

59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.title: Earnings Dynamics under Firm Heterogeneity
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.author: Timo Virtanen
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.summary: We develop a permanent–transitory earnings process in which permanent shocks depend on a latent firm type and workers’ exposure to firm types is persistent. Persistence can substantially slow the finite-horizon attenuation of earnings skewness and excess kurtosis over the life cycle relative to an iid mixture benchmark. We estimate the model from matched employer-employee data, first grouping firms based on the distribution of residual earnings changes and then using worker transitions across groups to estimate persistence. Finnish data reveal heterogeneity in permanent-shock variances and persistent exposure to firm groups. Although skewness and excess kurtosis are not targeted in estimation, over ages 35–50 the extended model accounts for 49 percent of average empirical skewness and 39 percent of average excess kurtosis, compared with 4 percent and 3 percent under the iid benchmark. Quantitative exercises show that persistence increases the life-cycle cost of earnings risk and affects saving behavior.

59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.title: Informal Work as a Fallback: Vision Impairment, Employment, and Policy in Brazil
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.author: Marcio V. Correa
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.summary: Informal work may allow workers with functional limitations to remain employed when formal jobs become too costly to hold, rather than reflecting exclusion from good jobs. In Brazilâ€™s 2019 Pesquisa Nacional de Saude, severe but partial vision impairment is associated with a formal employment rate 20.9 percentage points lower than among individuals with no difficulty, but with no difference in informal employment. The asymmetry survives adjustment for observables and other functional limitations, and it is not shared by mobility, upper-limb, or mental limitations. These patterns alone cannot reveal where affected workers would go if informal work were unavailable, or how policy would reallocate them. To answer these questions, we build a general-equilibrium incomplete-markets model in which individuals choose among formal work, informal work, and non-employment. Informal work is less productive, while formal work carries a rigidity cost that rises with functional limitation. We calibrate the model to occupational shares across four vision states. In the model, eliminating informal work lowers employment by 17.6 percentage points among individuals with a vision limitation. In illustrative counterfactuals, policies that reduce informality send workers to different destinations: stricter enforcement into non-employment, workplace accommodation into formal jobs, and broader disability-benefit eligibility into supported non-employment. Changes in informality are therefore an unreliable guide to the effects of disability and formalization policy.

59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.title: Do Firms Know What Workers Want?
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.author: Max Müller
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.summary: Labor supply depends on wages and amenities, and standard models implicitly assume that firms hold accurate beliefs about workers’ amenity valuations. In a survey with firms and workers in Germany linked to administrative data, we measure workers’ valuations of five different amenities and firms’ beliefs about workers’ valuations. We find that firms systematically underestimate workers’ valuations of all five amenities. These misperceptions are driven by interpersonal projection: managers project their own preferences—they value amenities less—onto workers. Through the lens of a simple model of imperfect competition, we show that firm misperceptions result in (i) labor shortages and (ii) excess labor costs for biased firms. Empirical tests confirm these predictions: a simple calibration suggests that non-providing firms could reduce their labor costs by 5% by providing amenities.

59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.author: Ana Popovici
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.title: The Long-Term Mental Health Consequences of Emotional and Interpersonal Work Demands
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.author: Vincent Vandenberghe
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.summary: This paper examines how career-long emotional/interpersonal work demands are associated with mental health among adults aged 50 and older. Using retrospective work histories from SHARE combined with ISCO-4-level occupational characteristics from O*NET, we construct employment trajectories capturing cumulative exposure to emotionally/interpersonally demanding work and examine its association with later-life depressive symptoms, measured by the EURO-D scale. Our findings show that careerlong emotional/interpersonal demands are associated with a higher risk of depression after age 50, although their relative importance is modest. Career instability, such as employment gaps, redundancies, and part-time work, emerges as a stronger predictor. Pre-labour-market factors, including childhood health and educational attainment, also play a substantial role, highlighting the lasting importance of early-life circumstances for later-life mental health.

59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.title: The Great Household Divergence - Economic Inequality and the Roots of Social Fracture for the 99%
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.author: Andrews, N. O.
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.summary: For decades, the debate over American inequality has centered on a single question: how unequal has the United States become? Increasingly, the more important question is different: does it matter that some Americans are pulling dramatically away from everyone else, even as real income rises for most people? This paper argues that the United States has undergone a Great Household Divergence: four decades of extraordinary prosperity coinciding with widening disparities in household market position â€” disparities that shape employment, status, dignity, health, and neighborhood opportunity. Economic distance has become social distance, accompanied by rising polarization and democratic strain. Mobility eroded for large segments of the population, leaving some American communities with world-class opportunity while others resemble the developing world. This paper weaves together literatures on inequality, mobility, polarization and social policy. It argues that the prevailing policy model has focused too heavily on correcting market outcomes after the fact, and points upstream toward pre-distribution policies that shape wages, collective bargaining, state-level employment institutions and macroeconomic conditions aimed at tighter labor markets. The central implication is that social cohesion in the U.S. cannot be restored through post-tax redistribution alone. Addressing inequality is more than the simple arithmetic of redistribution; it also requires attention to social cohesion, the earning power of Americans and human dignity.

59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.title: Which types of education raise firm productivity? Evidence for managers and workers in the UK
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.author: Hall, Tessa
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.summary: This paper estimates the firm productivity returns to degree field, institution quality, and degree level, and compares them with wage returns. I link a LinkedIn panel from Revelio Labs to Orbis financial accounts for over 20, 000 UK firms over 2015?2024. Within firms, a bachelor's degree raises a worker's productivity by around 20%; a top-20 institution adds a further 10% and a postgraduate qualification 6%. The returns differ by organisational role. A bachelor's degree raises productivity for managers and non-managers alike. Specialist credentials - a STEM field, an elite institution - raise productivity for non-managers but not for managers, whose premium loads instead on postgraduate qualifications, above all MBAs. Managers also contribute around 26% more than otherwise identical non-managers, a premium that education does not explain. Averaged over the workforce, wage premia are close to productivity premia for each type of degree. However, the average conceals two wedges of opposite sign: STEM-trained non-managers are paid below their relative productivity, and degree-holding managers above it. Finally, for a subset of firms matched to the World Management Survey, workforce education accounts for around a quarter the well-documented correlation between management practices and productivity.

59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.author: Hellsten, Mark
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.author: Xu, Yaling
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.author: Xiaoqing Zhou
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.summary: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.title: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.author: Camilo Morales-Jimenez
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.summary: The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.title: Do Pension Reforms Affect Migrants Differently? Evidence from Germany and Spain
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.author: Hao Wei
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.summary: This paper examines whether migrants and native-born workers respond differently to pension reforms that encourage longer working lives. Using longitudinal data from SHARE Waves 4â€“9 for Germany and Spain, we construct individual reform exposure based on country-specific reform timing, birth-cohort eligibility, and proximity to retirement age, and estimate models with individual and survey-wave fixed effects. Reform exposure is associated with a lower probability of retirement, with suggestive evidence of an additional decline among migrants. This migrant differential is particularly pronounced in Spain, while the corresponding estimate is small and statistically insignificant in Germany, although formal cross-country tests do not establish a statistically significant difference between the two countries. Complementary analyses indicate that adjustment is concentrated around retirement ages rather than reflecting a broad increase in employment, while evidence for effects on mental health and generalized trust is limited. Overall, the findings suggest that migrants may respond differently to pension reform, but that these differences are concentrated at specific retirement margins and depend on the institutional context

59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.title: Exploitation Cycles: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics in Labor Markets with Predatory Employers
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.author: Rusch, Hannes
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.summary: Exploitative employers damage the very labor force on which they depend. Accordingly, this paper models exploitation and labor-force quality as a coupled dynamical system: exploiters spread when high-quality labor makes extraction profitable, but their success degrades the labor environment that sustains those profits. We show that this coupling generates persistent cycles rather than convergence toastable level of exploitation. Our policy extension shows that responsive enforcement can dampen these cycles, induce convergence, and improve welfare. We contribute by elucidating exploitation dynamics and demonstrating how eco-evolutionary methods can be applied to study labor markets on which employers compete with exploiters.

59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.title: Reconstructing the Pre-Industrial Occupational Structure of Swedish Parishes - Data and Methods, 1749–1855
59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.author: Sandgren, Fredrik
59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.summary: This paper reconstructs the occupational structure of 1720 Swedish pseudo-parishes between 1749 and 1855 using the data contained in Tabellverket, a unique collection of population and occupational records covering the country from the mid-eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century. The original Tabellverket records are characterized by an unsystematic coverage in time and space and across occupational categories, changes in parish and pastorate boundaries, and missing observations that have so far inhibited its use at the parish level. We develop a procedure for transforming these records into a balanced panel data. The resulting dataset provides for the first time parish-level estimates of employment for 11 categories for the entire period 1749-1855 and 43 more detailed categories for the period 1805-1855 for both genders for 27 benchmarks, establishing a new empirical basis for studying long-run structural change in pre-industrial Sweden.

59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.title: Slave raiding in the twentieth century
59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.author: Rusch, Hannes
59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.summary: Slave-making and trading lastingly shaped global demographics. However, no quantitative studies of enslavement as a day-to-day business exist. We address this gap using a unique dataset coded from the surviving records kept by notorious slave raider Hamman Yaji (c. 1863–1929). Spanning fifteen years and over 300 events, the data reveal whom Yaji targeted, how he timed his raids, and how destructive they were. Panel regression analyses show how Yaji’s decisions were shaped by political, military, ecological, and economic constraints on profit maximization. Situated in colonial eastern Nigeria, our results provide unprecedented insight into the microeconomics of slave raiding

59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.title: Immigrant-Native Wage Gaps and Rent Sharing: A Segmented Assimilation Story?
59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.author: Mélanie Volral
59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.summary: Although an increasing body of literature has examined the relationship between firms’ profitability and wage inequality in the context of a diverse workforce, the role of rent sharing in explaining origin-based wage differentials has yet to be explored. Our paper aims to fill this gap using detailed Belgian matched employer-employee data from 1999 to 2016. After controlling for a wide range of covariates and addressing endogeneity issues, our estimates show that the wage-profit elasticity equals approximately 3% and does not differ statistically between native and immigrant workers, be they first or second generation. It therefore appears that firms share their profits equally with their employees, regardless of their origin. However, Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions suggest that rent sharing has a significant influence on immigrants’ wages through labour market segregation. Specifically, first-generation immigrants are found to earn lower wages than natives because of their higher concentration in firms with lower profit margins. The same is true for second-generation immigrants, but almost half as much. These findings, corroborated and refined by heterogeneity tests according to gender, educational attainment and level of collective bargaining, support the hypothesis of a segmented assimilation process for immigrants.

59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.title: Sorting into entrepreneurial teams
59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.author: Marta Morazzoni
59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form.

59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.title: Female Jobs and Fertility: Long-term Experimental Evidence from Ethiopian Factories
59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.author: Getahun, Tigabu
59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.summary: We conducted an experiment with multiple factories in Ethiopia to test the widespread hypothesis that formal employment among women reduces fertility. Tracking respondents over eight years, we find that women who were randomly offered a job had more children than the control group. The effect on fertility emerged once the effect on wage employment faded away, around three years after baseline. There are clear effects on household income and savings, but not on bargaining power or marriage. These patterns are consistent with a Beckerian model in which the income effect dominates the substitution effect and households are credit constrained.

59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.title: Lacunes en matière de compétences des travailleurs selon la perception des employeurs
59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.author: Genevieve Dufour
59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.summary: This report uses data from Statistics Canada’s Survey of Employers on Workers’ Skills (SEWS) to provide an overview of the skills sought, available, and developed within Canadian businesses. It focuses in particular on basic mathematics skills, numeracy, critical thinking, and problem-solving, comparing Quebec with Ontario and the rest of Canada. Our results show that basic mathematics skills are rarely perceived as a skills gap by businesses, both in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada. Quebec businesses, however, place relatively greater emphasis on technical, managerial, and computer skills, and less emphasis on critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication, both when recruiting and when developing employees’ skills. The results also show that Quebec businesses differ in how they manage skills. They assess their skills needs less frequently, make less use of informal skills-development practices such as mentoring and feedback, and report greater recruitment difficulties, regardless of the level of education required. Across all three regions, more than half of businesses attribute these difficulties to a lack of interested applicants, suggesting that job attractiveness is as much an issue as an actual shortage of skills. Finally, when faced with skills gaps, businesses tend to favour internal work reorganization rather than investing in human capital development. Ce rapport utilise les données de l’Enquête auprès des employeurs sur les compétences du personnel (EECP) de Statistique Canada pour brosser un portrait des compétences recherchées, disponibles et développées dans les entreprises canadiennes. Il porte une attention particulière aux compétences mathématiques de base, aux capacités de calcul, à la pensée critique et à la résolution de problèmes, en comparant le Québec à l’Ontario et au reste du Canada. Nos résultats montrent que les compétences mathématiques de base sont rarement perçues comme une lacune par les entreprises, au Québec comme ailleurs…

59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.title: Return-to-Work Policies for Disability Insurance Recipients: The Role of Financial Incentives
59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.author: Ilan Tojerow
59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.summary: This paper studies how financial incentives shape labor supply decisions among disability insurance (DI) recipients who already combine benefits with part-time work. We exploit a distinctive feature of the Belgian Adapted Work Program, in which DI benefits are progressively withdrawn as earnings increase and the marginal withdrawal rate rises sharply at predefined thresholds. Because participants cannot freely adjust their working hours, this setting allows us to estimate how higher implicit taxation affects transitions out of partial work. Using administrative data and a Regression Kink Design, we find that higher implicit tax rates induce exits in two opposite directions: toward full-time employment and back to full DI. A oneeuro increase in the implicit marginal tax per working day raises the probability of returning to full DI by 3.0 percentage points and of resuming full-time employment by 1.5 percentage points, corresponding to elasticities of 0.84 and 0.85. A simple labor supply framework rationalizes these divergent responses. Our findings show that the financial design of partial-benefit schemes can determine whether partial work serves as a bridge toward full employment or instead leads recipients back to full benefit dependency.

59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.title: Beyond Employment: Minimum Wage Effects on Hours Worked
59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.author: Hikaru Ota
59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.summary: This study estimates the effect of minimum wage increases on low-wage employment and working hours using an event study analysis based on 138 state-level minimum wage changes in the United States. The results show that employment declines in wage bins below the new minimum wage are largely offset by increases in employment at and above it, yielding a near-zero net employment effect. Applying the same wage bin framework to total usual weekly working hours, the analysis finds no significant reduction in total working hours. However, hours worked per worker decrease significantly in the wage bin at the new minimum wage. This pattern may reflect firms adjusting along the intensive margin, but it may also arise from changes in the composition of workers within that wage bin; the analysis cannot distinguish between these explanations. Nevertheless, the findings demonstrate that stable employment levels can mask underlying changes in hours worked.

4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.title: Anchor or sinker – Large firms, anchoring capacity and regional development
4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.author: Nilsson, Magnus
4a32a2255e:1af0f5ebbc4a0e6d.summary: This paper ties together two literatures which explain regional anchoring from different perspectives. One is based on the role of large organizations in anchoring an industry in a region, the other is systemic and deals with anchoring processes that circulate and embed knowledge. Each leaves implicit what the other explains. The aim is to understand how anchor effects and regional anchoring capacity interact across different regional contexts. Illustrative cases from three Swedish regions show how the two both diverge from and reinforce each other, anchor without anchoring and anchoring without an anchor, depending on regional configuration and anchor control.

4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.title: Multi-View Representation Learning for Regional Opportunity Spaces and Industrial Path Development
4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.author: Grillitsch, Markus
4a32a2255e:d9d5b6345d7baa90.summary: Regional opportunities for industrial development arise when local conditions favor particular economic activities. These conditions depend in part on a region’s existing industry profile and on the economic relationships among its activities. Heterogeneous data sources on mobility, production, and firm ownership provide complementary evidence about this underlying industrial structure. We therefore develop a multi-view representation-learning framework for industries that integrates these different sources into a shared latent representation. By using graph diffusion, the framework captures both direct and indirect connections between industries. Applied to Swedish industries over three decades and three classification versions, the learned representation places industries from different classification periods within a common latent space. To evaluate this operationalization of opportunity, we construct an opportunity-density measure by combining latent similarity with local industry size. Higher opportunity density is consistently associated with industry entry and startup formation and with lower industry exit. Across classification periods, a one-standard-deviation increase in opportunity density is associated with 5.3–6.2 percentage-point higher industry-entry probabilities (118–136% of baseline rates), 8.9–13.8 percentage-point lower industry-exit probabilities (147–209%), and 1.1–1.7 percentage-point higher startup-formation probabilities (131–187%). Opportunity density remains associated with these outcomes in 41 of 42 models after accounting for information contained in the individual data sources. Our machine-learning framework shows how heterogeneous data can be integrated into a common latent structure and used to operationalize regional opportunity spaces, providing a new approach to studying industrial path development.

4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.title: The Costs of Access: Freeway Disamenities Across U.S. Cities
4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.author: Jeffrey Lin
4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.summary: We construct city-level measures of freeway disamenities and examine their association with metropolitan growth. We combine neighborhood-level estimates from Brinkman and Lin (2024) with calibrated spatial models for U.S. metropolitan areas. Each city measure is based on a counterfactual that removes estimated disamenities while holding modeled travel times fixed. Cities with larger estimated disamenities grew more slowly, conditioned on total freeway mileage and initial population. Total freeway mileage is positively associated with growth in the same specification. Estimated disamenities are larger in cities with greater 1950 populations, more centralized freeway networks, and coastal geography. These patterns are consistent with local quality-of-life costs attenuating regional access related growth benefits.

4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.title: Agglomeration, the Price-Index Effect, and Migration in Post-NAFTA Mexico
4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.author: Keisuke Kondo
4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.summary: This study examines how multiple agglomeration and dispersion forces shaped Mexico’s regional economic geography during the early post-NAFTA period. When economic activity becomes geographically concentrated, consumers gain better access to differentiated varieties and face lower effective transport costs, reducing the local consumption price index and making a region more attractive as a migration destination. Building on this price-index mechanism from New Economic Geography, we focus on four spatial forces: proximity to the U.S. market, the manufacturing price-index effect, the service price-index effect, and density-related urban costs. Using bilateral interstate migration between 1995 and 2000, we proceed in two stages. First, we estimate the structural parameters of the model and recover state-level price indices for manufactured goods and services. Second, we examine how destination–origin differences in nominal wages, price indices, and urban costs are associated with migration across sectors, while controlling for the additional locational advantage of U.S. border states. The manufacturing price index is strongly and negatively associated with migration of manufacturing workers, whereas its cross-sector effects are more limited. By contrast, the service price index is negatively and significantly associated with migration across all sectors, indicating a broad domestic agglomeration force. Employment density is generally negatively associated with migration, consistent with urban costs acting as a centrifugal force, while real-wage differentials are positively associated with migration across most industries. Taken together, the findings suggest that post-NAFTA Mexico was shaped by the interaction of border-oriented manufacturing agglomeration, domestic service-sector agglomeration, and urban-cost-driven dispersion.

4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.title: University as catalyst of public R&D expenditures? An empirical assessment on EU NUTS 3 regions
4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.author: Saverio Barabuffi
4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.summary: This study examines whether universities shape the regional innovation effects of public R&D expenditure and whether this role varies across regional development trajectories. We analyse a panel of 1166 EU NUTS 3 regions over the period 2007-2020, combining data on European public R&D funding, patenting performance, university presence and regional development traps. Toa ddress the endogeneity of public R&D expenditure, we employ a control function aproach. The results show that public r&D expendirue positively affects patenting performance in both university and non-university, but the difference between them is not statistically significant. University presence therefore does not sistematically amplify the returns to public R&D. However, its moderating role becomes more pronounced in regions exposed to development trap risk and in regions experiencing persistent stagnation, while evidence is weaker for trap intensity. These fundings suggest that universities act as contingent rather than unviersal catalyst of public R&D. Their contribution appears particularly relevant in vulnerable and persistently stagnant regional trajectories, but less able to offset sever structural constraints. The study contributes to debates on the geography of public R&D and regional development traps by showing that the effectiveness of research funding depends not only on institutional presence, bu also on the development rajectory in which that institutional capacity is embedded.

33e1d7779a:8082b8e3489a250e.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:8082b8e3489a250e.summary: The FAA is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:5d47aab2d4b87b6e.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday. Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology. Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees. Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12 , requesting they appear. The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations. Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed. What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release . A representative for Huang did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International. Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips. Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies. The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and…

33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.title: Jensen Huang says he'd be "honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:70054ab4672706c2.summary: Jensen Huang acknowledged in a statement to the Wall Street Journal that he'd be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Why it matters: A push to reinstate Huang began almost as soon as he exited the company, but Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating the former CEO, according to multiple reports. What they're saying: "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." State of play: A slew of candidates have been mentioned across multiple analyses and reports about the Nvidia successor. President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook for the role. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look for outside candidates. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is currently serving as the company's acting interim CEO. Editor's note: This is a breaking story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:af8ebd3cedf11692.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders. What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed. Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research. (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.) Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups: Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder. The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses. Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said. Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming…

33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.title: Hakeem Jeffries shifts tactics ahead of House Democrats' internal speaker vote
33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:dd86484486845238.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) plans to force his members to take a tallied vote this week on whether to nominate him as speaker of the House, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Why it matters: The plan represents a shift in tactics — his allies had previously hoped to nominate him by acclamation — that would help reveal whether he has the votes to become speaker on Jan. 3. If he loses more than 40 votes, he may be in trouble. If not, he likely sails through even if some of his members ultimately oppose him on the House floor. Jeffries and his allies are confident he has more than enough support to get the 218 votes needed to become speaker even as some of his freshman members express skepticism or even outright opposition to him. "Jeffries will win," a senior House Democrat told Axios. Jeffries' plans were first reported by Punchbowl News. Between the lines: This new strategy would exploit the fact that, as of Tuesday, no other House Democrat has announced their candidacy for speaker. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who is often floated as a possible alternative in constituent phone calls to lawmakers urging them not to back Jeffries, told Axios he is not running for speaker. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), who has become the focus of a recent draft movement, has also told allies she is not interested in the role, as Axios previously reported. Pressley, asked about running for speaker at a town hall event in her district on Monday, told attendees : "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." State of play: House Democrats are set to meet behind closed doors starting Wednesday morning to elect their leadership team for the 120th Congress. In addition to nominating a candidate for speaker, they are set to vote on electing a House majority leader and whip, an assistant speaker, and a Democratic caucus chair and vice chair, among other leadership positions. Most of the candidates for those senior roles are…

33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:8402278f32eb9f02.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more…

33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.author: Carly Mallenbaum
33e1d7779a:b16d704e72abfd3d.summary: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:93bdc8eb0df6e1c4.summary: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100…

33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:6b256a6ce0839fc0.summary: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have…

33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.title: Democrats' squishy definition of Medicare expansion
33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:e20dd7a20ce30e4d.summary: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other…

33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.title: Trump's biggest project is running out of time
33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:8f9f0823954db4d4.summary: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would…

33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.title: Florida stayed red in a blue wave. But look at what happened in Hispanic precincts.
33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.author: Sommer Brugal
33e1d7779a:84ce1146103b038d.summary: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35)…

33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.title: U.S. allies on edge as Trump heads to summit with Xi and Putin
33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:ff99fa484e81b09b.summary: President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious. Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios. Substance aside, Western diplomats worry about the optics of Trump appearing alongside two emboldened strongmen. On Monday, Trump also floated a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?" But other topics will get attention, too, Trump went on to say. "We'll talk about Iran. We have Iran in very good shape, but we'll talk about Iran a little bit," he said. The president also said "we'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine." His comments came after U.S. officials stressed in a call with reporters on Friday that the summit would not deal with the war in Ukraine. Chinese officials said the same thing. Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine. Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat. Some of…

33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.title: Top Trump aides to meet with Europeans, Ukrainians on peace plan
33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:ced3d5cccecfc0ba.summary: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to meet with Ukrainian and European officials this week to work on security guarantees and a postwar economic recovery plan for Ukraine, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The Thursday meeting in Berlin comes a week after Witkoff and Kushner urged Russia to propose a postwar security framework for Europe — a parallel effort they hope will help bring the war to a close. On the same day, Trump will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China. Trump said on Monday that he expects to talk about the war in Ukraine. Zoom in: The aim of the Berlin meeting is to develop security guarantees to deter future Russian attacks on Ukraine as well as plans to rebuild its economy, the official said. The Trump aides have been in regular contact with Ukrainian and European officials as they engage Russia simultaneously, the person said. The U.S. official described the Berlin meeting and Trump's visit to China as a coordinated diplomatic effort. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — who are joining Trump in China — have been briefed on the Ukraine negotiations, the person said. Zoom out: Witkoff and Kushner met with Putin in Moscow last Thursday. They also spoke Monday with his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the war talks. Axios reported last week that the U.S. asked Russia for a European security proposal that includes steps by Moscow to ease tensions. Many European governments, however, are highly skeptical that Russia would honor any agreement. Earlier this month, Axios reported that the U.S. hoped easing Russian diesel sanctions would win concessions, but Putin still rejected a ceasefire. The big picture: One overarching question is whether Europe will participate directly with Russia in negotiations to resolve the war. Witkoff and Kushner said Russia agreed that…

33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.title: Jordan inherits House GOP fight over punishing rebels
33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:3c7fccd5ae28a517.summary: One of House GOP Minority Leader-elect Jim Jordan's first challenges will be navigating a push by Republicans to punish members who buck party leadership. Why it matters: Jordan, a founding member of the House Freedom Caucus, is now tasked with leading a conference where lawmakers are seeking to rein in the very tactics his conservative allies have long used to challenge GOP leadership. The conference will consider a number of amendments and rules when it organizes in a few weeks. Discussions are ongoing, a source familiar with Jordan's thinking tells Axios. Driving the news: Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) and members of the Republican Main Street Caucus want to punish members who vote against the party on procedural rule votes , a technical vote that conservatives have repeatedly used as a hostage-taking tactic. Main Street's proposal would empower the Steering Committee to impose penalties ranging from loss of committee seniority to "more serious" consequences. Leadership or the chair of the relevant committee would then implement Steering's decision. Flood told Axios that Main Street members developed the proposal collectively over several months, including through a survey and multiple meetings. Flood and other Republicans pushing accountability measures have been in contact with Jordan's team as they work to finalize their proposals. The big picture: House Republicans' razor-thin majority gave every member outsized leverage over GOP leaders this Congress. One consequence has been repeated defeats on procedural votes that used to be automatic for the party. That has derailed GOP priorities and, on must-pass bills, left GOP speakers dependent on Democratic votes instead of legislation supported by their conference. Main Street's proposal would restore a small piece of that leverage by letting Steering leaders punish members who block those votes. "This has nothing to do with telling a member how to vote on an issue," Flood said of the proposal. Zoom in: House…

33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.title: United Airlines resolves "widespread system outage" that delayed flights
33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.author: Donica Phifer
33e1d7779a:b81275929fb927ab.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it resolved what it called a "widespread system outage" that delayed departing flights for about 90 minutes. Why it matters: It was a quick resolution to yet another issue affecting the U.S.' beleaguered airspace, which spent days digging itself out of thousands of flight delays and cancellations following Friday's hours-long ground stop . What they're saying: "We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience. We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United Airlines wrote on X in reply to a customer. "We appreciate your patience while we work through this. Please check back with us for updates, and keep an eye on your flight status through the United app or at http://united.com . Thanks for bearing with us!" The customer said the issue stemmed from planes being unable to determine weight limits, though United did not confirm that was the problem. United Airlines told Axios that the company is "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights." "There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights. There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," they said. About an hour and fifteen minutes after United posted its apology, the company tweeted again to say the issue was resolved and encouraged passengers to check their flight status at the company's website. United gave no additional information about what caused the outage, and it's unclear how many flights were impacted. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

33e1d7779a:12fb50528067520d.title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
33e1d7779a:12fb50528067520d.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:12fb50528067520d.summary: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that…

33e1d7779a:a2e513e28efacd9c.title: What we know about what caused the FAA's nationwide ground stop
33e1d7779a:a2e513e28efacd9c.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:a2e513e28efacd9c.summary: A newly installed router is at the center of the investigation into the Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop last Friday, which disrupted thousands of flights nationwide.
