"They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader." Zoom in: Opposition to Schumer has been building: "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from her party leadership. Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen, who is also considering a 2028 presidential run, said he's been listening to calls for him to challenge Schumer and considering his options.

Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the…

He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have…

33e1d7779a:d458fdcc5ba7a2f5.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.author: Van Reenen, John
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.author: Xu, Yaling
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.author: Asani Sarkar
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.author: Collin B. Raymond
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.author: Daniel Herbst
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.title: Productivity review of the Netherlands: Supporting business dynamism to revive productivity growth
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.author: OECD
b3ea4f41ab:7c080b908a305ced.summary: The Netherlands has one of the highest levels of labour productivity in the OECD, but growth has slowed over the past decade. The slowdown partly mirrors global trends but has been accentuated by weak investment and declining business dynamism. Against this background, this paper provides a cross-country comparative analysis of the role of firm entry, exit, growth and resource reallocation across firms, in shaping recent Dutch productivity performance. A set of policy simulations suggests that, even though the country performs well on a wide range of policy indicators, some reforms could boost business creation and job reallocation, thereby lifting productivity. The most promising measures include streamlining labour legislation, upgrading education and training, reducing the administrative burden on start-ups, refining the insolvency regime and further encouraging R&D and venture capital investment.

b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.title: Transforming Textile Waste into Circular Value: Innovation, Community Participation and Sustainable Entrepreneurship in Micro and Small Enterprises
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.author: Sweta Patnaik
b3ea4f41ab:5832b279f95538ba.summary: In an era marked by economic uncertainty and environmental urgency, entrepreneurs are increasingly turning to sustainable innovation as a pathway to resilience and growth. This paper examines how the transformation of textile off-cut waste into functional and marketable products serves as both an entrepreneurial response to material scarcity and a strategic contribution to the circular economy. In contrast to high-capital technological innovation, this form of resource-based creativity offers accessible, low-cost solutions for emerging enterprises, particularly in the fashion and textile sectors. Drawing on examples of micro and small businesses navigating uncertain economic terrain, the study highlights how such innovations can generate value, reduce waste, and meet growing consumer demand for sustainability. While many entrepreneurs falter in the face of early challenges, those who reframe problems as opportunities particularly through material reuse are better positioned to survive and scale. This paper argues that innovation rooted in environmental consciousness and adaptability is not only viable during times of uncertainty but essential for long-term entrepreneurial success and inclusive economic recovery.

b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.title: Current state and development prospects of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan: From an emerging market to a systemic driver of economic growth
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.author: Malika Azimova
b3ea4f41ab:399cb4b09b29ab56.summary: This article examines the institutional and economic conditions shaping the development of franchising in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Drawing on an analy-sis of the legal and regulatory framework, industry statistics, field research, and comparisons with selected international markets, the study identifies the main fac-tors limiting the sector's growth and proposes a phased model for its institutional development. Particular attention is given to regional disparities, the sectoral composition of the market, and the potential of locally developed franchise sys-tems to support entrepreneurship and expand employment opportunities. The empirical evidence covers the period 2024?2025 and includes an analysis of commercial concession agreements as well as expert interviews with market par-ticipants from eight regions of Uzbekistan.

b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.title: Heterogeneous Firms, Growth and the Long Shadows of Business Cycles
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.author: Adam Hal Spencer
b3ea4f41ab:6a6cf025f7cc45bd.summary: Do ï¬ rms differ in their innovation response to business cycles? What economic forces shape this heterogeneity? And does it matter for aggregate propagation? We document substantial heterogeneity in ï¬ rm-level R&D cyclicality, develop a theory to explain this fact, and validate its key mechanism in the data. In a tractable model of business cycles and innovation-driven growth, endogenous selection makes R&D particularly responsive to aggregate conditions for ï¬ rms close to the exit margin. Consistent with this mechanism, ï¬ rms closer to exit display more procyclical R&D in the data. Quantitatively, selection and endogenous growth interact powerfully: selection generates heterogeneous R&D cyclicality, while endogenous growth translates these heterogeneous responses into persistent aggregate effects. Ignoring heterogeneous R&D cyclicality misses roughly half of the long-run output cost of a severe recession.

b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.title: Women Artisans in Economic and Social Development: A Systematic Literature Review on Entrepreneurship, Cultural Heritage, and Empowerment
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.author: Yingying Zhang Zhang
b3ea4f41ab:47c0143a0dd77ed0.summary: Introduction: Women artisans play a crucial role at the intersection of cultural heritage, entrepreneurship, and rural development, acting as preservers of age-old traditions and catalysts for community economic growth, although the scientific literature on this phenomenon remains fragmented. Objective: To synthesize and analyze existing evidence regarding women artisans, focusing on their roles as agents of economic development, preservers of cultural heritage, and drivers of social empowerment initiatives. Method: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA methodology, involving searches in the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Following a screening process, 30 studies were analyzed using both bibliometric and hermeneutic approaches. Results: Systemic barriers-such as limited access to finance and sociocultural restrictions-were identified alongside effective facilitators, such as cooperatives that generate income growth. Conclusions: Women's artisan entrepreneurship constitutes an integrated model of sustainable development that links personal empowerment, cultural preservation, and economic growth. Women artisans act as agents of social transformation, creating impacts that extend beyond their own lives to benefit entire communities.

b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.title: Sorting into entrepreneurial teams
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.author: Marta Morazzoni
b3ea4f41ab:82a934767f3d67c7.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form.

b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.author: Asani Sarkar
b3ea4f41ab:daeafea108d23544.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.title: Breaking into Supply Chains : Experimental Evidence on Procurement Training for Women-Owned SMEs
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.author: Neelamraju, Kalyan N.
b3ea4f41ab:6735834859328ccf.summary: Women-owned-or-led small and medium-sized enterprises (WSMEs) are underrepresented in public and corporate supply chains worldwide. There is growing interest in promoting SMEs’ and WSMEs’ integration into value chains, but limited causal evidence whether interventions to support their participation in procurement are effective. This paper conducts a phased randomized controlled trial to estimate the impacts of corporate procurement training for WSMEs in Colombia. The program increases procurement knowledge and readiness, resulting in a ten percentage point increase in registrations to corporate portals, and an eight percentage point increase in the likelihood of submitting a bid. Impacts on winning bids are concentrated in WSMEs with prior procurement knowledge or experience, whose probability of winning a contract increases by eight to nine percentage points. These impacts are approximately twenty percent of the control means. More broadly, the paper illustrates how complier-weighted treatment effects can be used to evaluate programs delivered through a funnel-shaped participation process, common in private sector development interventions.

18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.title: University as catalyst of public R&D expenditures? An empirical assessment on EU NUTS 3 regions
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.author: Saverio Barabuffi
18d1edb9f2:f67930276d86a5c4.summary: This study examines whether universities shape the regional innovation effects of public R&D expenditure and whether this role varies across regional development trajectories. We analyse a panel of 1166 EU NUTS 3 regions over the period 2007-2020, combining data on European public R&D funding, patenting performance, university presence and regional development traps. Toa ddress the endogeneity of public R&D expenditure, we employ a control function aproach. The results show that public r&D expendirue positively affects patenting performance in both university and non-university, but the difference between them is not statistically significant. University presence therefore does not sistematically amplify the returns to public R&D. However, its moderating role becomes more pronounced in regions exposed to development trap risk and in regions experiencing persistent stagnation, while evidence is weaker for trap intensity. These fundings suggest that universities act as contingent rather than unviersal catalyst of public R&D. Their contribution appears particularly relevant in vulnerable and persistently stagnant regional trajectories, but less able to offset sever structural constraints. The study contributes to debates on the geography of public R&D and regional development traps by showing that the effectiveness of research funding depends not only on institutional presence, bu also on the development rajectory in which that institutional capacity is embedded.

18d1edb9f2:32337b243ef6525a.title: Regional Dynamics of Innovation in Europe 2000-2020 A Tale of Convergence, Persistence, and the Illusion of Catch-Up
18d1edb9f2:32337b243ef6525a.author: Michael Wyrwich
18d1edb9f2:32337b243ef6525a.summary: This study examines the dynamics of regional innovation activity in Europe from 2000 to 2020 using patent applications. Standard convergence measures indicate that regional disparities are narrowing, with initially lagging regions catching up to the leading ones. Our analysis reveals two persistent â€˜clubsâ€™: the â€˜laggingâ€™ and the â€˜advancedâ€™ regions. Although these groups are becoming increasingly similar, the differences between them remain largely unchanged. Despite two decades of growth, the disparity between the two clubs still accounts for a great deal of the total variation in regional patenting. These patterns suggest a convergence illusion that is overlooked in the current scholarly debate.

18d1edb9f2:72996851f5c1a5a7.title: An experimental study on the effect of knowledge on idea generation and idea selection
18d1edb9f2:72996851f5c1a5a7.author: Stoczek, Rika
18d1edb9f2:72996851f5c1a5a7.summary: How firms generate and select ideas influences their strategic path and the development of entire industries. To better understand this process, we experimentally analyze the impact of knowledge on idea generation and selection in an incentivized ideation task. Between treatments, we vary whether or not ideators are provided with examples of previous successful ideas before working on the task. We provide causal evidence that knowledge about such example ideas leads to path dependencies, i.e., knowledge increases the similarity of new ideas to those provided. Consistent with the hypothesis that knowledge affects the search for new ideas, we find evidence of path dependencies during idea generation, but do not find statistically significant evidence of additional path dependencies during idea selection. Overall, when knowledge is provided, we observe an increase in selected innovative ideas that are similar to previous ideas and a decrease in selected innovative ideas that are different from previous ideas.

18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.title: Arenas of Change: Towards sustainable material flows
18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.author: Stihl, Linda
18d1edb9f2:08227758a80d9e92.summary: The sustainability imperative calls for a sharp reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and virgin materials use. This requires the transformation of currently unsustainable global and linear value chains (GVCs) to regenerative and circular supply chains (CSCs). To deal with the complexities of such a shift, this paper suggests Arenas of Change as a theoretical perspective and methodological approach, capturing interaction spaces of actors who engage in changing how goods are produced, distributed and consumed, and how waste is recovered and reduced. Actors are conceptualised as being embedded in multi-scalar network, institutional and governance structures, which can enable or hinder change processes. We argue that the possibility of Arenas of Change to effectuate and accelerate shifts from GVCs towards CSCs depends on the realisation of synergies in four domains: i) business logics, models, and innovation; ii) consumption and user practices, iii) modes of governance, and iv) policies and discourses. Arenas of Change are thus a prism through which the interdependencies between domains, multiple scales and levels, and actors' strategies can be analysed. Thereby, Arenas of Change can contribute to theory-building about transformations from global and linear to regenerative and circular supply chains, and conditions that enable, accelerate or hinder such systemic change. Furthermore, by enhancing analytical leverage to comprehensively capture the complexity of such transformations, we propose Arenas of Change as an approach to design impactful interventions, and to evaluate their effects.

18d1edb9f2:d960b7bbcf837d85.title: Unpacking the selection environment: Directionality shaped by emerging valuation ecosystems
18d1edb9f2:d960b7bbcf837d85.author: Hoekman, Jarno
18d1edb9f2:d960b7bbcf837d85.summary: Arguing against techno-determinism remains one of the cornerstones of innovation studies. Scholars have relentlessly shown how social conditions and strategic choices determine the pace and direction of technological development, supporting the idea that innovation can be steered towards societal goals such as economic competitiveness, employment or sustainability. Most scholarly attention, however, focused on the processes that generate new varieties of products and technologies, while the selection environment determining their direction is left largely unspecified. In this paper, we draw on insights from economic sociology to propose a conceptual framework for unpacking key structures and mechanisms of the selection environment through which societal values act upon technology development during periods of normative contestation. Central to our approach is the concept of valuation devices, understood as the organizational forms and material infrastructures embedded in institutional arrangements through which values are attributed to technologies and products. Beyond identifying these devices as strategic vehicles for actors to steer technology development, we show how they conjointly constitute a valuation ecosystem that shapes the directionality of a field. This framework is applied to the European food packaging sector, where proliferating health and environmental concerns have spurred a range of technological trajectories characterised by diverging strategies and goals. We retrace how actors advance distinct valuation devices to address evolving concerns about food packaging, and how the emerging valuation ecosystem shapes directionality by structuring corridors of legitimate innovation pathways. The paper concludes that deeper conceptual engagement with the selection environment opens promising new research perspectives for innovation studies.

fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:97d3780fdbff4a98.summary: Organisations face a trade-off when appointing and delegating power to middle managers. On the one hand, the manager may take decisions that are not beneficial to the organisation. On the other hand, the manager may have better local information. In multi-ethnic countries this trade-off shapes whether the organisation may want to appoint a manager co-ethnic to the market served or co-ethnic to the organisation itself. This is studied in the context of Ethiopia, where an unexpected civil war increased the salience of ethnicity.

fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.title: Episode 107: Cristobal Otero on the Effect of Managers on Public Hospital Performance
fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:10eb88327ee6e17c.summary: This paper studies the effect of managers for the performance of public hospitals, specifically following a reform in Chile that changed their recruitment process. The main findings are that the reform decreased mortality, likely through the mechanism of improving the quality of managers (e.g., replacing managers without management degrees with managers with management degrees).

fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.title: Episode 106: Alexia Delfino and Miguel Espinosa on Value Dissonance at Work
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:6efc59758fb1d8a7.summary: This paper studies what happens when a worker has a different set of values than (a) their boss, or (b) their colleagues. Productivity is lower workers with such value dissonance, and the mechanism appears to be worse worker morale and worse communication between worker and manager.

fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.title: Episode 105: Michael Frakes on Doctor Diversity and Racial Health Differences
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:9e3018f394a3b4a7.summary: This paper studies whether the racial diversity of medical providers (mostly doctors) in the hospital, affects the health outcomes of minority patients. There is a big effect and, most importantly, it does not only operate through the concordance between individual patient and individual doctor: having more diverse doctors in the hospital generates positive externalities that go beyond the patient-doctor relation.

fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.title: Episode 104: Victoria Angelova on the Comparison between Algorithms and Humans Making Decisions
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.author: Jordi Blanes i Vidal | The Visible Hand
fd826003ba:999aee89b4154734.summary: This paper studies whether human decision-makers can improve on algorithmic recommendations, in the setting of bail decisions in the criminal justice system. Bail judges receive recommendations from predictive algorithms and can choose to confirm or override them. The paper finds that most judges do not add value beyond the algorithm, although a minority do.

f3fd1ffa24:dbf4ff0e1e4b1a71.title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
f3fd1ffa24:dbf4ff0e1e4b1a71.summary: Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market's opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper , we track what happened to stock investors' perceptions of a bank's risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023 . We find that, after a first trip to the Fed's Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank's weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

f3fd1ffa24:4a93cf67344f3221.title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?
f3fd1ffa24:4a93cf67344f3221.summary: Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.

f3fd1ffa24:1fa93dbff6be7665.title: Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update
f3fd1ffa24:1fa93dbff6be7665.summary: As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago .

f3fd1ffa24:1754a7c07a755517.title: A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
f3fd1ffa24:1754a7c07a755517.summary: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

f3fd1ffa24:f15416153b845e47.title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
f3fd1ffa24:f15416153b845e47.summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.author: Thomas Klitgaard
f3fd1ffa24:8c142c33b72c8379.summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.author: Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli
f3fd1ffa24:f264753704ee9bc6.summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.title: How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.author: Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner
f3fd1ffa24:c48a20582dc18d57.summary: In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.

f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.title: Evaluating New LinkedIn Labor Market Tightness Indicators
f3fd1ffa24:a4402c9f2991db79.summary: Measures of labor market tightness (LMT) describe how difficult it is for firms to find workers. The labor market is considered tight if there are few job seekers available relative to job openings, implying stronger wage pressures as employers compete for scarce job seekers. Thus, good measures of LMT are important for predicting wage inflation and calibrating monetary policy. Recently, the hiring platform LinkedIn began producing three innovative LMT measures based on its user data. In this post, we use public data from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to evaluate the ability of these novel measures to predict wage and price inflation relative to existing LMT measures, finding that one stands out as particularly useful and timely.

f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
f3fd1ffa24:42008bb79cf11289.summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.author: Julian di Giovanni
f3fd1ffa24:22a1cb8ad31be2ec.summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
f3fd1ffa24:45d0a3bff02d5db0.summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
f3fd1ffa24:2fd0334d84f65de0.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Response of Investment to Monetary Policy
f3fd1ffa24:00bc17cbb1a550c2.summary: It is well known that monetary policy affects firms’ investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report , we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect.

f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.author: Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise, and David E. Weinstein
f3fd1ffa24:60233756dac81b20.summary: There has been a lot of interest in how tariffs affect consumer prices (for example, Cavallo et al. 2021 , 2025 ). In this post, we present results from our new research paper that estimates the effects of the 2025-26 tariffs on retail consumer prices. We find that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year. Roughly two-thirds of the effect arises because tariffs raise the prices of imported consumer goods. The remaining third arises indirectly: tariffs increase the prices of goods made in the U.S. because producers pay more for imported parts and materials, and because producers raise their markups when competing imports cost more. The effects differ in their timing. Prices of imported goods respond quickly to tariffs, while prices of U.S.-made goods adjust over six to twelve months as higher costs move through the supply chain.

f3fd1ffa24:91124a79f6cc5b49.title: Insured, but Still on the Hook: Who Bears the Most Risk in Homeowner’s Insurance?
f3fd1ffa24:91124a79f6cc5b49.summary: In an April post , using millions of homeowners' insurance contracts matched with property-level exposure and disaster risk, we showed that although households are insured, they are still "on the hook” because deductibles and coverage limits leave homeowners responsible for part of a loss. Because insurers cannot perfectly observe how well homeowners maintain or protect their properties (a problem known as “moral hazard”), contract terms such as deductibles can play an important role in balancing risk sharing and incentives. By requiring homeowners to bear part of a loss, insurers can preserve incentives for policyholders to take actions that reduce damage risk. In this post, we quantify the cost of keeping homeowners on the hook. How costly is moral hazard in homeowner's insurance? How much risk must households retain to preserve these incentives? And, importantly, who ultimately bears that residual risk? The short answer is that keeping homeowners on the hook costs insurers relatively little, but it leaves households with substantial risk, especially those least able to absorb a large loss.

91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.title: Are Nonprofit Tax Exemptions and Deductions "Federal Financial Assistance"? Should They Be?
91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.author: Lloyd Hitoshi Mayer
91cd3b3295:85b9892d1c6fbdb2.summary: Two recent federal court decisions have reignited the debate over whether “Federal financial assistance” as used in four federal anti-discrimination statutes includes the tax benefits enjoyed by most nonprofit organizations. Both courts concluded that it does. While an appellate court reversed one decision, and the other case settled without appellate review, these holdings create significant uncertainty. And this uncertainty affects the more than 1.8 million tax-exempt nonprofits, many if not most of which do not receive federal financial assistance through other channels and so could safely conclude these statutes do not reach them, absent these decisions. This uncertainty is also magnified by recent Trump administration assertions that nonprofits and other private entities receiving federal financial assistance must conform to that administration’s views of what constitutes illegal discrimination. This Article first considers whether the two recent decisions were correct in deciding that federal financial assistance in this context includes nonprofit tax benefits and determines that the weight of authority strongly supports the conclusion that they were not. More specifically, it reviews the relevant statutory language, existing regulatory and other administrative guidance, and court decisions and commentary addressing this issue to reach the conclusion that “Federal financial assistance” as used in Title VI, Title IX, the Rehabilitation Act and the Age Discrimination Act does not include the exemption from federal income tax enjoyed by most nonprofits and, for charities, the eligibility to receive tax-deductible contributions. This Article also considers the contrary arguments asserted by courts and commentators and explains why none of those arguments are persuasive. This conclusion does not end the matter, however, as those same arguments suggest that Congress should expand the reach of these anti-discrimination statutes to include nonprofits that enjoy…

91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.title: Redemption! Valuing Closely Held Companies After Connelly
91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.author: Adam Chodorow
91cd3b3295:4a6f4c3df37c1c37.summary: In Connelly v. United States , the Supreme Court resolved a long-standing dispute over how to treat redemption obligations when valuing a decedent’s shares in a closely held company. The Court held that redemption obligations do not offset corporate-owned life insurance proceeds obtained to fund a redemption, upsetting a long-standing practice. While the Court undoubtedly reached the right conclusion, it (1) failed to address important arguments the parties and amici raised; (2) assumed away the effects of discounts, premiums and different valuation techniques, which would have complicated the analysis without changing the conclusion; and (3) muddied the water somewhat by leaving open the possibility of a different outcome where companies use operating assets to fund a redemption. This Article lays out the various authorities that bear on this question, sets forth additional grounds supporting the Court’s conclusion, including the arguments the Court sidestepped, addresses the complexities avoided by using a simple hypothetical and explains why the reasoning applies equally to situations where operating assets are used to fund a redemption. Finally, the Article identifies different ways taxpayers can use insurance to fund redemptions while avoiding the results in Connelly .

91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.title: State Tax Discrimination and Internal Consistency
91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.author: Michael T. Fatale
91cd3b3295:773fe8a2e2df3085.summary: The contours of the U.S. Supreme Court’s dormant Commerce Clause doctrine of internal consistency, which asks whether a state tax intrinsically overreaches in imposing a burden upon interstate commerce, are difficult to understand. This is despite the fact that a determination that a state tax violates internal consistency can have significant state fiscal consequences. This uncertainty was suggested again by the recent case, Zilka v. Tax Review Board City of Philadelphia , for which the Supreme Court later denied certiorari. See 304 A.3d 1153 (Pa. 2023), cert. denied , 145 S. Ct. 1045 (2025). The parameters of the internal consistency doctrine should not be so obscure. The doctrine would be more logical and understandable if it were primarily utilized, not as a stand-alone test, but as a tool to evaluate state tax discrimination, i.e., whether a state has impermissibly sought to favor local businesses over businesses based in other states. This Article explains how this approach would be more firmly grounded in the Court’s current approach to the dormant Commerce Clause and, for example, would be consistent with the Court’s “undue burden” balancing inquiry as recently reconsidered in National Pork Producers Council v. Ross , 143 S. Ct. 1142 (2023). This Article also sets forth how this analysis would comport with the Supreme Court’s prior internal consistency cases, including Comptroller of the Treasury of Maryland v. Wynne , 575 U.S. 542 (2015), and recent state court cases applying the internal consistency test.

91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.title: The Mother of All Tax Shelters
91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.author: Michael Doran
91cd3b3295:76817f675a4a9bf5.summary: By its own account, the federal government spends more than $500 billion every year to subsidize retirement savings in 401(k) plans, IRAs and similar arrangements. That figure is larger than the annual budget of every government agency other than the four largest. The theory behind this massive subsidy is that it gives workers at all income levels an incentive to save money that they would otherwise spend, thereby enhancing retirement security, reducing old-age poverty and easing dependence on Social Security. But the theory is wrong. The retirement tax subsidy is anything but egalitarian. Less than five percent of the subsidy goes to households in the bottom 40 percent of the income distribution scale, and more than 60 percent goes to households in the top 20 percent. And among higher-income households, the subsidy generally does not encourage saving. Instead, the affluent respond to the subsidy primarily by moving assets from taxable investment accounts to tax-exempt retirement accounts. In short, the federal government spends more than half a trillion dollars every year to provide windfalls to higher-income households with little meaningful increase in retirement security for lower-income and middle-income households. It is time to acknowledge that the retirement tax subsidy is a tax shelter, nothing more and nothing less, and to reset tax policy accordingly.

91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.title: The Chilling Effect of SFFA v. UNC/Harvard on Race-Based Affirmation by Tax-Exempt Charities
91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.author: David A. Brennen
91cd3b3295:ab26e9eb371960ca.summary: Recently, the Supreme Court decided in SFFA v. Harvard/UNC that colleges are restricted in their use of race-based affirmative action in admissions. Post- SFFA , many have incorrectly suggested that this means that race may never be considered in admissions. This Article asserts that this expansive view of SFFA is incorrect and leads to a chilling effect on affirmative action by colleges. However, instead of simply asserting that SFFA permits some considerations of race in admissions, the Article goes further by arguing that SFFA does not even apply to admissions by some private colleges. For instance, private colleges that are recipients of federal financial assistance(FFA) must abide by SFFA because of Title VI, which is essentially synonymous with the Equal Protection Clause. But what if a private tax-exempt actor decided to forgo FFA? Could such private actor then lawfully use race-based affirmation action in light of SFFA ? The Article concludes that, even after SFFA , colleges may continue to consider race in admissions to a limited extent. Further, private tax-exempt charities that don’t receive FFA are not subject to SFFA ’s restrictions. Thus, private charities may use race-based affirmative action in admissions—even if such use goes beyond what’s permitted by SFFA .

c7a9af4a79:aac60ddd4c9b68c1.title: What's Mine Is Mine: Taxing Pre-Contribution Gains
c7a9af4a79:aac60ddd4c9b68c1.author: Rodney P. Mock et al.
c7a9af4a79:aac60ddd4c9b68c1.summary: This article conducts an analysis of the Internal Revenue Code's varied income tax treatment between depreciated property and appreciated property transferred into C corporations by shareholders in nonrecognition transactions.7 It is at the entry point of the non-recognition transaction where the lobster pot unfairly doubles up on unrecognized gains at both the corporate and shareholder level notwithstanding that unrecognized losses generally remain singular at either level. The authors call into question this long-standing practice of artificial gain duplication upon corporate entry under Subchapter C. From a tax policy perspective, such disparate treatment makes little sense - particularly when the duplicated gain is not economically associated with the corporate solution (i.e., it was incurred pre-contribution). To properly appreciate the differing income tax treatment between pre-contribution gains and losses, the first part of this article explores the corporation as a separate taxpaying entity distinct from its shareholders, the lack of a coherent rational behind the double tax system, and the phantom gain enigma associated with pre-contribution gains. The next part of this article discusses the operation of Subchapter C with regard to formation, capital contributions, non-liquidating distributions, and liquidating distributions. We then discuss the general purpose behind Congress' enactment of the loss limitation provisions and how we arrived at the current state of the law where pre-contribution losses generally remain singular while pre-contribution gains are duplicated. We conclude by making certain suggestions primarily designed to eliminate the gain duplication quagmire, such as a partial imputation system or a modified full integration system.

c7a9af4a79:020df82cf48ceb57.title: Helvering v. Gregory: All the Perspectives from which Learned Hand Was Wrong
c7a9af4a79:020df82cf48ceb57.author: Anthony P. Polito
c7a9af4a79:020df82cf48ceb57.summary: At a fundamental level, this Article is about interpretation. The best way for a court to remain faithful to a complicated statute reflecting a delicate legislative compromise is to enforce its language literally without introducing extraneous tests or elements that cannot be found in the statutory language. Yet, it is important to be clear that it approaches the question from an ex ante perspective, from where things stood before Learned Hand's famous opinion. This Article is not a call for the judicial reversal of Hand's opinion. Given the value of the predictability of established expectations as to statutory meaning, stare decisis is at its strongest when applied to statutory interpretation. The business purpose requirement is now reflected in a Treasury Regulation that is entitled to a high degree of deference. Congress has had multiple opportunities to eliminate it and has not so done. No, this Article is not an argument for the judicial reversal of a familiar old decision. It advances the claim that, as of the time the court faced the decision, the outcome it selected was incorrect from multiple policy perspectives and therefore a counterproductive exercise of the interpretive authority. Moreover, at the time decided, it was a mistaken use of the interpretive authority to upset a carefully set legislative compromise in favor of the court's own preferred outcome. Before proceeding, a further caveat is necessary. Although the Supreme Court upheld Hand's opinion unanimously, this Article focuses primarily on Hand's opinion for the Second Circuit for good reasons. His is the more frequently quoted of the two opinions. His opinion is the more extensive of the two. It sets out more thoroughly the justification for creating a business purpose requirement, while the Supreme Court opinion largely relies on its reference to Hand's opinion.

c7a9af4a79:c718befbd47fcc29.title: PFICs Gone Wild!
c7a9af4a79:c718befbd47fcc29.author: Monica Gianni
c7a9af4a79:c718befbd47fcc29.summary: This Article begins in Part II with a discussion of what constitutes a passive foreign investment company ("PFIC") and follows in Part III with the tax rules applicable to PFICs. Part IV begins with a general explanation of the goal of tax deferral, with discussion of several anti-deferral tax regimes enacted prior to the PFIC provisions, i.e., Personal Holding Companies ("PHCs"), Foreign Personal Holding Companies ("FPHCs"), Subpart F income of CFCs, Foreign Investment Companies ("FICs"), and Regulated Investment Companies ("RICs"). An understanding of these regimes is necessary to appreciate the genesis of the PFIC rules. Part V analyzes the policy behind Congress enacting the PFIC provisions as part of the Tax Reform Act of 1986,9 i.e., preventing U.S. investors in foreign investment companies from having more favorable tax treatment than U.S. investors in domestic investment companies. Congress wanted to correct the perceived abuses of U.S. taxpayers investing in foreign investment companies to obtain U.S. tax deferral on their investments and close the gap in previously enacted legislation. After a crash course in the basic PFIC rules and other anti-deferral regimes, and an understanding of why the rules exist, Part VI examines unexpected consequences of the PFIC rules. PFIC treatment, although targeted to stop abuses with foreign investment companies, can reach start-up and operating companies. In addition, otherwise nontaxable transfers can be subject to tax, such as an exchange of PFIC stock in a tax-deferred reorganization, a gift of PFIC stock during life and upon death, and taxation to immigrants and expatriates who own PFIC stock. Transfers of PFIC stock can result in disastrous consequences to the unsuspecting (or even the suspecting) investor, a result that seems to go beyond what Congress intended when it enacted the PFIC legislation. Part VI additionally addresses specific solutions for these problems. The simple purpose of not allowing tax…

c7a9af4a79:8896489455e7a48a.title: Why Congress Adopted the Church Audit Procedures Act and What Must Be Done Now to Restore the Law for Churches and the IRS
c7a9af4a79:8896489455e7a48a.author: J. Michael Martin
c7a9af4a79:8896489455e7a48a.summary: This Article explores the significant policy purposes achieved by CAPA through the lens of the law's history and present challenges. Part II reviews the historical context and events leading to the adoption of CAPA in 1984. Part III then describes the present challenges associated with the law due to the failure of Congress and the Treasury Department to rectify the issue of who is an appropriate high-level Treasury official under CAPA. Finally, Part IV concludes with recommended solutions for restoring the law consistent with congressional intent in adopting CAPA-solutions that could easily be achieved through a simple amendment to the statute by Congress or similar regulations issued by Treasury.

c7a9af4a79:6dabc27d1e635255.title: Give Taxpayers a Break: Putting the Reliance Element Back into the Reasonable Reliance and Good Faith Defense
c7a9af4a79:6dabc27d1e635255.author: Ronald Z. Domsky
c7a9af4a79:6dabc27d1e635255.summary: This Article considers the present law regarding the accuracy related penalties pursuant to I.R.C § 6662 and the reasonable reliance and good faith defense provided for in I.R.C § 6664 using Canal as a prime example of how the courts have treated and penalized taxpayers for relying on tax advisors in planning proposed transactions and in taking positions on returns and proposes a new analysis of a taxpayer's good faith and reasonable reliance. Section II of this Article discusses the current state of the law regarding the Section 6662 penalties, the function and regulations imposed on tax attorneys in advising taxpayer clients, the Section 6664 good faith and reasonable reliance defense, and provides an overview of the facts and legal analysis underlying the Tax Court's holding in Canal. Section III analyzes the current law and presents a new analysis of a taxpayer's good faith and reasonable reliance on his attorney's advice and opinions that should be implemented by the IRS and the courts, which comports with all current law, including the Circular 230 requirements imposed on tax practitioners generally. Section IV will conclude this Article.

1fadfd23b2:ceff918dbb2cd942.title: Elite Law Firms Are Leaving Their Rivals Behind
1fadfd23b2:ceff918dbb2cd942.author: Bloomberg Law
1fadfd23b2:ceff918dbb2cd942.summary: A new study from Chambers and Partners reveals that the most elite, fastest-growing law firms, such as Kirkland & Ellis and Latham & Watkins, are seeing a compounding of their success — and the window is narrowing for other firms to catch up. On this episode of On the Merits, Chambers CEO Tim Noble and Chief Data Innovation Officer Lisa Hart Shepherd discuss this first ever report crunching the millions of data points Chambers has collected over the past decade about the top 100 law firms. “So, we found that there was a huge disparity in performance,” Shepherd said. “You’ve got firms that are growing well over a hundred percent over the period, and we’ve got a few that are declining and everything in between.” Shepherd said the top performers excelled in premium practices and offered a distinctive client experience. READ MORE: Chambers Advantage Index Firms that were growing quickly but don’t have the scale or reputation of the top firms — firms such as Polsinelli and McGuireWoods — need to find an advantage to compete, Noble said. “Targeting talent” is a possible path for these firms to reach the top tier, he said, but these firms are going to need to make “transformational moves” to catch up.

1fadfd23b2:938a9cea1d90b2ec.title: When Winston Met Taylor: US-UK Firm's Chief Looks to Bridge Gaps
1fadfd23b2:938a9cea1d90b2ec.author: Bloomberg Law
1fadfd23b2:938a9cea1d90b2ec.summary: "Culture" is a popular buzzword for law firm leaders describing in vague terms what sets them apart from their rivals. For Winston Taylor's Steve D'Amore, it's a key part of melding the two firms that combined in June in Big Law's latest transatlantic merger. "We put culture at the top of the list of things that were important to make sure we had right," D'Amore said on Bloomberg Law’s podcast, On The Merits. That includes blending US and European approaches to consensus building and urgency to attain "urgent collaboration" across the newly minted $1.75 billion firm, he said. Chicago's Winston & Strawn and UK firm Taylor Wessing hired BDO Global to analyze cultural compatibility before the merger was announced and brought the consultants back to look at pain points after completing the tie-up, D'Amore told Bloomberg Law reporter Roy Strom. Winston Taylor's leaders are also trying to bridge gaps on lawyer pay, client conflicts, practice group structures and AI tools. Do you have feedback on this episode of On The Merits? Give us a call and leave a voicemail at 703-341-3690.

1fadfd23b2:0446934f61cfbdba.title: Baker McKenzie Head: Law Firm Billing Should Be Ready to Move On
1fadfd23b2:0446934f61cfbdba.author: Bloomberg Law
1fadfd23b2:0446934f61cfbdba.summary: AI is changing the way the legal profession operates and everyone — lawyers, law firms, and especially clients — needs to look past the institution that is the billable hour, according to Baker McKenzie global chair Sunny Mann. “We all need to collectively move on in our thinking to get alternative fee arrangements working in the right way," he said on Bloomberg Law's On The Merits podcast. Mann spoke to Bloomberg Law reporter Roy Strom about how his firm is using AI to change its relationship with its clients, the role AI played in its recent layoffs of professional staff, and what it's like for him to lead a global law firm during a time when globalization may be on the wane. Do you have feedback on this episode of On The Merits? Give us a call and leave a voicemail at 703-341-3690.

1fadfd23b2:ab721aaf0fa84a01.title: Sidley Leader Yvette Ostolaza Shares Growth Strategy
1fadfd23b2:ab721aaf0fa84a01.author: Bloomberg Law
1fadfd23b2:ab721aaf0fa84a01.summary: Sidley Austin LLP crossed $3.74 billion in revenue last year and has its sights set on $4 billion — but according to its top leader, the number is a byproduct, not the goal. The real question is whether the firm is built for what comes next. Today on On the Merits: Yvette Ostolaza, chair of Sidley's management committee, sits down with Bloomberg Law reporter Meghan Tribe to discuss strategic lateral hiring, formal integration plans, and a willingness to pull back from practices and geographies that aren't growing. "There are no sacred cows," Ostolaza said. "We need to continue to evaluate how the industry is changing." She also weighed in on how Sidley is treating AI: not as a pilot project, but as core leadership infrastructure deployed across the firm with dedicated governance, training, and practice-group liaisons. "It doesn't replace judgment, it sharpens it," Ostolaza said.

1fadfd23b2:aeafd481630e3960.title: K&L Gates Goes on the Offensive in the Legal Talent Wars
1fadfd23b2:aeafd481630e3960.author: Bloomberg Law
1fadfd23b2:aeafd481630e3960.summary: When it comes to winning the legal industry talent wars, the best defense is a good offense, according to K&L Gates' global managing partner, Stacy Ackermann. Her firm is "going out into the market" rather than "being in a reactionary mode of 'Let's see what comes to us and what the headhunters bring to us,'" Ackermann said. She spoke to Bloomberg Law editor Chris Opfer on our podcast, On The Merits, about how competitive the market for legal talent has gotten, even in secondary markets like her home base of Charlotte, N.C. She also talked about why K&L Gates is continuing to push its attorneys to use AI, even after some of its attorneys got reprimanded last year for using hallucinated citations in a court case. "I remember not so long ago that clients would say to me 'Please tell me you're not using AI,'" Ackermann said. "And now they're saying to me 'Please tell me you are using AI.'" 57a95411f6:b6481603652e7c6f.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:b6481603652e7c6f.summary: Can habeas corpus cases proceed as class actions? The Supreme Court has never squarely answered that question, even in cases where lower courts certified habeas classes. But the Trump Administration’s wholesale push to expel noncitizens has forced the question to the center of modern civil rights litigation. The post Habeas Class Actions appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.title: Indigenous Constitutionalism
57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.summary: By standard accounts, there are fifty-four constitutions across the federal, state, and territorial governments of the United States. But in fact, there are 230 other governmental constitutions that currently govern peoples and territories within the United States. These constitutions not only flow from a sovereignty that existed prior to the United States but also came out of a legal movement that asserted its independence from both the U.S. Constitution and state constitutions. This Article tells the story of these constitutions — the constitutions of Native nations. The post Indigenous Constitutionalism appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.title: What is a Tort?
57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.summary: What is a tort, and what is tort law for? On one leading scholarly account, torts are legal liability rules that seek to promote the welfare of society at large by disincentivizing socially suboptimal behavior and distributing the costs of accidents to those who can best bear them. The post What is a Tort? appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.title: Drug Scheduling as Institutional Design
57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.summary: The United States makes bad choices when it comes to psychoactive drugs. Under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), U.S. drug law has simultaneously fueled mass incarceration, inhibited needed access, and enabled an opioid crisis. The post Drug Scheduling as Institutional Design appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.title: Practical Consequences in Statutory Interpretation
57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.summary: Modern textualism has long criticized the use of practical, or consequentialist, reasoning when construing statutes. And yet in practice, textualist jurists long have invoked practical consequences arguments to help justify their statutory constructions. Fieldhouse, Karel Mertens American Economic Review How much does public research funding raise inventive activity? Evidence from U.S. appropriations shocks uses budget variation to identify the returns to government R&D. The estimates link funding changes to subsequent innovation, providing causal evidence on the public contribution to technological advance. How Effective Are R&D Tax Incentives? Reconciling the Micro and Macro Evidence Silvia Appelt, Matěj Bajgar, Chiara Criscuolo, Fernando Galindo-Rueda American Economic Journal: Economic Policy Recent firm-level studies find R&D tax incentives to be much more effective at stimulating firms’ R&D investment than aggregate analyses suggest. Based on a distributed analysis of official R&D survey and administrative tax relief microdata for 19 OECD countries, shows that two factors can reconcile these contrasting results. First, the limited uptake of R&D tax incentives in most countries makes aggregate studies underestimate the effectiveness of R&D tax incentives. Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape Steven Callander, Nicolas S. Lambert, Niko Matouschek American Economic Journal: Microeconomics How do competition and innovation interact when technologies are unevenly connected? A theoretical model represents technological search on a rugged landscape with firms choosing innovation under competitive pressure. The results characterize how market structure changes incentives to explore, the variety of innovations, and long-run performance. Innovation booms, easy financing, and human capital accumulation Johan Hombert, Adrien Matray Journal of Financial Economics What happens to workers attracted into a technology boom by high wages? Linked French worker and firm data track the late-1990s ICT expansion and subsequent careers. High-skill entrants experience persistent earnings losses consistent with faster skill obsolescence rather than selection or the sector’s bust; abundant financing disproportionately reaches firms whose workers later suffer the largest productivity declines. Vertical Mergers With Bilateral Contracting and Upstream and Downstream Investment Mark Israel, Daniel P. O'Brien Journal of Economics & Management Strategy Can vertical integration improve complementary investments? A double-moral-hazard model of private bilateral contracts shows mergers reduce bargaining externalities and hold-up. Consumers and unintegrated downstream rivals benefit when products are sufficiently close or distant substitutes; at intermediate differentiation, consumer gains depend on sufficiently low investment costs, with an application to the computer industry. Patently peculiar: Patents and innovation in the United Kingdom of the Netherlands Homer Wagenaar, Christopher L. Colvin Economic History Review How did discretionary patent administration support early industrialization? Hand-collected applications from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, 1815–1830, distinguish invention patents from protection for imported technologies. Administrators applied novelty and utility screening while encouraging useful technology transfer; despite high fees, access extended across social classes without evidence of systematic discrimination. 22e8cdb80c:82fe4a1f2c12b775.title: Useful Knowledge Issue No. 021 - October 20, 2026
22e8cdb80c:82fe4a1f2c12b775.summary: Issue No. 021 30 papers. Growing Pains: Inefficient Resource Allocation in Emerging Economies Li Anpeng International Economic Review Why can fast technological catch-up coexist with inefficient resource allocation? A model combines firm-specific technology adoption with costly adjustment of production inputs. Rapid progress increases the need to move resources from slow to fast adopters, magnifying adjustment frictions; Chinese and German enterprise data imply development-stage differences explain at least 40% of their labor-allocation efficiency gap. Subsidies for innovative technology adoption: Experimental evidence on malaria in Burkina Faso Elodie Djemaï, Yohan Renard Journal of Health Economics Do subsidies increase adoption and sustained use of a new malaria-prevention technology? A randomized experiment with 3,120 households in Burkina Faso compares no subsidy with 50% and 100% subsidies. Subsidies increase both uptake and regular use, supporting affordability as a barrier to adoption rather than the claim that charging more necessarily improves use.
